stem: Which sentence needs commas?
options / answer: A) We saw lions. | B) Lions roar. | C) We saw lions tigers and bears. | D) We saw lions and tigers.
why correct: Three items in a series need commas: lions, tigers, and bears.
tip: Count the items. Three or more? Use commas.

stem: What does unhappy mean?
options / answer: A) happy again | B) happy before | C) very happy | D) not happy
why correct: The prefix un- means not.
tip: Cover the prefix, read the base word, then add the prefix meaning.

stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
options / answer: A) friend | B) frind | C) freind | D) frend
why correct: Friend is spelled f-r-i-e-n-d.
tip: Memory trick: a friend to the end.

stem: A story about a soccer final is told by the goalkeeper who let in the winning goal. How would the description of the final minute most likely change if the scorer narrated it?
options / answer: A) It would describe the goalkeeper's thoughts in detail. | B) It would focus on excitement and pride instead of disappointment. | C) It would include no feelings at all. | D) It would describe exactly the same feelings.
why correct: A narrator's point of view shapes which feelings and details are emphasized.
tip: RL.5.6: ask how the narrator's experience colors the events.

stem: A text explains that honeybees pollinate crops, that bee numbers are falling, and that farmers are planting wildflower strips to help. Which statement best captures BOTH main ideas?
options / answer: A) Honeybees make honey. | B) Wildflowers are pretty. | C) Bees are essential to farming, and people are acting to reverse their decline. | D) Farmers grow many crops.
why correct: Grade 5 texts can have two main ideas: why bees matter, and how people help them.
tip: Check that your summary statement covers every section.

stem: “The early bird catches the worm.” Which situation shows this proverb?
options / answer: A) A bird ate a worm in the garden. | B) Omar slept late and missed the bus. | C) Lina likes birds more than worms. | D) Noura arrived first at the book sale and found the rarest book.
why correct: The proverb means people who act early get the best opportunities.
tip: Match the proverb's lesson to a real-life example.

stem: Which sentence correctly combines the ideas using a dependent clause? “It was raining. We played inside.”
options / answer: A) Because it was raining, we played inside. | B) It was raining because we played inside. | C) Because it was raining. | D) It was raining, we played inside.
why correct: Because it was raining is a dependent clause that explains why.
tip: Put the cause in the because-clause.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The students forgot | there | notebooks in the library.
why correct: Their shows ownership (the students' notebooks); there tells where.
tip: their = belongs to them; there = place; they're = they are.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: Which word is a common noun?
options / answer: A) Dammam | B) teacher | C) Ms. Amal | D) Friday
why correct: Teacher names a general person, not a specific one.
tip: Common nouns are not capitalized unless they start a sentence.

stem: What kind of sentence is this? “Please close the window.”
options / answer: A) declarative (a statement) | B) exclamatory (strong feeling) | C) imperative (a command) | D) interrogative (a question)
why correct: Imperative sentences give commands or requests.
tip: Declarative . | Interrogative ? | Exclamatory ! | Imperative (command).

stem: Which word is a synonym for begin?
options / answer: A) pause | B) finish | C) forget | D) start
why correct: Begin and start mean the same thing.
tip: Swap the words in a sentence: if the meaning stays, they're synonyms.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which word is an adjective? “A tall building shone brightly.”
options / answer: A) tall | B) building | C) shone | D) brightly
why correct: Tall describes what kind of building.
tip: Adjectives answer: what kind? which one? how many?

stem: Which word is more formal than kids?
options / answer: A) folks | B) children | C) guys | D) buddies
why correct: Children is the formal, standard word.
tip: Use formal words in reports and essays.

stem: Which claim would require the strongest evidence to be convincing?
options / answer: A) Many teachers assign reading homework. | B) Some students prefer homework on weekends. | C) Homework has no effect on student learning at any grade level. | D) Homework can help students practise skills.
why correct: Absolute claims (“no effect,” “any grade”) need broad, strong evidence because one counterexample can disprove them.
tip: The bigger the claim, the stronger the evidence it needs.

stem: In a story, a girl lies to protect her friend; the lie grows, the friendship nearly breaks, and she finally confesses. The friend forgives her. Which theme is developed MOST fully?
options / answer: A) Protecting friends is more important than anything. | B) Friends should never forgive each other. | C) Lying always works out in the end. | D) Honesty, even when difficult, is necessary for trust between friends.
why correct: The plot moves from a lie, to consequences, to a confession that restores trust.
tip: RL.6.2: track how the theme develops through particular details.

stem: A writer wants readers to admire a character who rarely gives up. Which word should the writer choose?
options / answer: A) determined | B) inflexible | C) stubborn | D) pigheaded
why correct: Determined has a positive connotation for not giving up.
tip: Choose words whose feeling matches your purpose.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: Between you and | I, | the test was easy.
why correct: Between is a preposition, so it takes the objective case: between you and me.
tip: After prepositions (between, for, with, to), use me, him, her, us, them.

stem: Which sentence correctly uses parentheses to set off nonessential information?
options / answer: A) The museum open (since 1985) attracts, thousands of visitors. | B) The museum (open since 1985) attracts thousands of visitors. | C) The museum (open since 1985 attracts) thousands of visitors. | D) The (museum open since 1985) attracts thousands of visitors.
why correct: Parentheses go around extra information that could be removed without breaking the sentence.
tip: Read the sentence without the parentheses—it should still make sense.

stem: What is the main problem in “The Stick Bridge”?
options / answer: A) Maya’s bridge breaks before the contest. | B) The class cannot find a dictionary. | C) Omar does not want to help Maya. | D) Maya cannot find any craft sticks.
why correct: When the bridge snaps at twelve seconds, Maya says, “It’s ruined.” That is the story’s problem.
tip: The conflict is the problem a character must solve. Look for the moment things go wrong.

stem: How is the problem in “The Stick Bridge” solved?
options / answer: A) Omar builds a different bridge by himself. | B) Maya and Omar replace the weak stick and add triangles. | C) The teacher lets Maya skip the contest. | D) Maya buys a new bridge kit from a store.
why correct: The story says they “replaced the weak stick and glued small triangles along both sides,” and the bridge holds.
tip: The resolution is how the problem is solved. Look near the end of the story.

stem: In “The Stick Bridge,” the problem is solved before the contest begins.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: They fix the bridge “that night,” and on Thursday it holds the dictionary for sixty seconds.
tip: Check when the fix happens compared with when the contest happens.

stem: Why does Maya say, “I don’t have time to start over”?
options / answer: A) Omar has hidden the craft sticks. | B) She has already finished her homework. | C) The contest is only two days away. | D) She has to go to bed right away.
why correct: The bridge breaks on Tuesday night and the contest is on Thursday, so there is little time.
tip: Use details about time and days to explain a character’s words.

stem: Put the events of “The Stick Bridge” in order.
options / answer: Omar finds a cracked stick. → The bridge snaps during a test. → Omar shows a picture of triangles. → The bridge holds the dictionary for sixty seconds.
why correct: The crack comes first, then the break, then the idea, and finally the success at the contest.
tip: Problem, attempts to solve it, and resolution usually happen in that order.

stem: How does solving the problem change Maya?
options / answer: A) She decides to build bridges only by herself. | B) She decides never to enter a contest again. | C) She decides that triangles are too hard to make. | D) She decides to listen more carefully to her brother.
why correct: Her last words are, “Next time, I’ll listen when you find a crack.”
tip: A character’s last words often show what they learned from the conflict.

stem: Which detail early in the story hints that the bridge will break?
options / answer: A) Omar finds a stick with a crack. | B) Maya spreads forty sticks on the table. | C) Maya reads the rules. | D) The contest is on Thursday.
why correct: The cracked stick is the piece that later snaps, so the author hinted at the problem early.
tip: Foreshadowing is a clue that hints at what will happen later.

stem: In “The Stick Bridge,” the cracked stick is a clue about what happens later.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Omar points out the crack, and later “It was the cracked stick” that broke.
tip: Notice details the author repeats later in the story.

stem: Why does the author show Maya tossing the cracked stick into the pile “without looking”?
options / answer: A) To show that Omar is wrong about the crack. | B) To show she is not paying attention, which leads to the problem. | C) To show that the contest is easy. | D) To show she is very careful with her work.
why correct: Her careless choice puts the weak stick in the bridge, and the bridge breaks because of it.
tip: Ask why the author included a small action. It often matters later.

stem: Which sentence from the story is foreshadowing?
options / answer: A) Maya grinned at Omar. | B) Sixty seconds passed. | C) “This one has a crack,” he said. | D) The bridge did not even wobble.
why correct: Omar’s warning comes early and points to the break that happens later.
tip: Foreshadowing appears before the event it hints at.

stem: In “The Pearl Diver’s Daughter,” Noura says she will count the stars “every night until you come home.” What does this suggest?
options / answer: A) Noura is learning about astronomy. | B) Her father will return the same night. | C) Noura is afraid of the dark. | D) Her father will be gone for a long time.
why correct: Counting stars every night hints at many nights of waiting during a long season.
tip: A character’s promise can hint at what lies ahead.

stem: An author writes: “The sky was clear, but the old fisherman kept looking at a small dark cloud in the west.” What is this most likely foreshadowing?
options / answer: A) A storm may come later in the story. | B) The fisherman will catch many fish. | C) The fisherman will move to the west. | D) The story will end at sunrise.
why correct: A clear sky with one worrying cloud, and a character who keeps watching it, hints at bad weather ahead.
tip: When a character keeps noticing something, the author may be preparing you for it.

stem: After Omar shows the picture of triangles, what will Maya and Omar most likely do?
options / answer: A) Build a tower instead of a bridge. | B) Use triangles to make the bridge stronger. | C) Start reading the math book. | D) Give up on the contest.
why correct: Omar says they need “stronger shapes” and shows a bridge made of triangles.
tip: Use what a character says and shows to predict what happens next.

stem: Based on the ending of “The Stick Bridge,” what will Maya most likely do in her next project?
options / answer: A) Use only broken sticks. | B) Work without anyone’s help. | C) Check her materials and listen to Omar’s warnings. | D) Skip reading the rules.
why correct: She says, “Next time, I’ll listen when you find a crack.”
tip: Predictions should match what a character has learned.

stem: At the end of “The Pearl Diver’s Daughter,” it makes sense to predict that Noura will keep the white shell safe.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Her father asks her to keep it, and she holds it to her ear as he leaves.
tip: A good prediction is supported by details in the text.

stem: Which detail BEST supports the prediction that Noura will miss her father?
options / answer: A) The dhows rocked in the harbor. | B) She had been five years old. | C) The summer sun was already hot. | D) She is “afraid of the empty months without him.”
why correct: Her fear of the empty months shows she will miss him while he is gone.
tip: Choose the detail that connects most directly to the prediction.

stem: Read: “Sami studied his spelling words every night and asked his sister to quiz him.” What is the BEST prediction?
options / answer: A) Sami will probably do well on his spelling test. | B) Sami will forget his spelling words. | C) Sami will stop studying tomorrow. | D) Sami’s sister will take the test for him.
why correct: Studying every night and practicing with a partner usually lead to success.
tip: Combine text clues with what you already know to make a prediction.

stem: Which TWO details help you predict that the bridge will hold at the contest?
options / answer: A) They glued triangles along both sides. | B) The contest was on Thursday. | C) Maya’s face felt hot. | D) They replaced the weak stick.
why correct: Removing the weak stick and adding triangles both make the bridge stronger.
tip: Look for details that show a problem has been fixed.

stem: When does “The Pearl Diver’s Daughter” take place?
options / answer: A) At night during a storm | B) In the summer of 1932 | C) In the present day | D) In the winter of 1932
why correct: The first paragraph names the season (summer) and the year (1932).
tip: Setting includes when a story happens. Look for years, seasons and times of day.

stem: Where does “The Pearl Diver’s Daughter” take place?
options / answer: A) In a busy city far from the sea | B) On a mountain farm | C) At the shore of a small town on the Gulf | D) Inside a school classroom
why correct: The story mentions the shore, the harbor and dhows in “her small town on the Gulf.”
tip: Setting includes where a story happens. Look for places and objects.

stem: Why is the setting important to the problem in this story?
options / answer: A) The hot sun makes Noura sick. | B) The town has no market for dates. | C) The harbor is too small for the dhows. | D) Pearling happens at sea, so Noura’s father must leave for months.
why correct: Because the story takes place in a pearling town in summer, her father must sail away for the season.
tip: Ask how the time and place cause or shape the characters’ problems.

stem: The word “dhows” helps show that the story is set in a place where people sail on the sea.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Dhows are wooden sailing boats, so the word shows that the setting is a seaside town.
tip: Special objects in a story are clues to its setting.

stem: How would the story be different if it were set in a desert town far from the sea?
options / answer: A) Noura’s father could not go pearling from that town. | B) Noura would be five years old. | C) Noura would not have a father. | D) The story would happen in the year 2032.
why correct: Pearling needs the sea, so the whole event of the story depends on the seaside setting.
tip: Imagine changing the setting. If the events no longer work, the setting is important.

stem: Which detail shows that the story takes place in the past?
options / answer: A) Noura has a father. | B) The town’s boats are wooden dhows with sails. | C) Noura packed some dates. | D) The sun is hot.
why correct: Wooden sailing dhows used for a pearling season, together with the year 1932, show a time long ago.
tip: Look for objects or ways of life that belong to a particular time.

stem: Which part of “The Pearl Diver’s Daughter” is a flashback?
options / answer: A) Noura packs a bag of dates. | B) Her father gives her a white shell. | C) Noura remembers being five and crying at the waves. | D) The dhow’s sail fills with wind.
why correct: The story jumps back to when “She had been five years old.” That is a flashback.
tip: A flashback interrupts the story to show something that happened earlier.

stem: A flashback tells about events that happened before the main story.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: A flashback goes back in time to an earlier event.
tip: Flash = quick; back = to the past.

stem: Which words signal that the story is moving back in time?
options / answer: A) “The dhow’s sail filled with wind.” | B) “Keep this,” he said. | C) “Now Noura was ten.” | D) “She had been five years old.”
why correct: “Had been” and the younger age show that we are hearing about an earlier time.
tip: Words like “had,” “remembered” and earlier ages signal a flashback.

stem: Why does the author include the flashback?
options / answer: A) To show that Noura once feared the sea but now fears missing her father. | B) To describe the market in the town. | C) To explain how pearls are made. | D) To show that her father is a good swimmer.
why correct: The memory contrasts her old fear of the waves with her new fear of the months without her father.
tip: Ask what the flashback helps you understand about a character now.

stem: What brings the story back to the present after the flashback?
options / answer: A) “From up there, the sea had looked like a sheet of blue glass.” | B) “Now Noura was ten, and she was not afraid of the sea.” | C) “She had stopped being afraid.” | D) “The waves had frightened her.”
why correct: The word “Now” and her present age (ten) return the reader to the day of the story.
tip: Look for words like “now” and “today” after a flashback.

stem: Put these events in the order they really happened in Noura’s life (not the order in which they are told).
options / answer: Noura cries at the waves when she is five. → Her father lifts her onto his shoulders. → Ten-year-old Noura walks to the shore. → Her father sails away on the dhow.
why correct: The flashback events happened five years before the day the father sails.
tip: A flashback is told later but happened earlier. Arrange events by time, not by page.

stem: How does Noura feel about her father leaving?
options / answer: A) Angry because he forgot her dates | B) Excited because she wants to go pearling | C) Sad and worried about the months without him | D) Afraid of the waves on the shore
why correct: She is “afraid of the empty months without him” and promises to count stars until he returns.
tip: A character’s perspective is how that character thinks and feels about events.

stem: How is Maya’s point of view different from Omar’s right after the bridge breaks?
options / answer: A) Maya thinks it can be fixed; Omar wants to quit. | B) Both think the contest is not important. | C) Both think the bridge is ruined. | D) Maya thinks the bridge is ruined; Omar thinks it can be fixed.
why correct: Maya says, “It’s ruined.” Omar says, “Maybe we just need stronger shapes.”
tip: Compare what two characters say about the same event.

stem: In “The Stick Bridge,” Maya and Omar react the same way when the bridge breaks.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Maya is upset and wants to give up, while Omar calmly suggests a solution.
tip: Read each character’s words carefully to find their point of view.

stem: How does Noura’s father seem to feel about leaving?
options / answer: A) Calm and caring, wanting to comfort Noura | B) Angry that Noura came to the shore | C) Uninterested in saying goodbye | D) Frightened of the sea
why correct: He kneels, takes her hand, smiles and gives her a shell so she will feel close to him.
tip: Actions can show a character’s feelings even when the character does not name them.

stem: Read: “Everyone cheered when the rain began, but Faisal stared at the soggy football field and sighed.” What is Faisal’s perspective?
options / answer: A) He is excited to play in the mud. | B) He is disappointed because the rain may stop his game. | C) He is afraid of thunder. | D) He is happy about the rain like everyone else.
why correct: While others cheer, Faisal stares at the field and sighs, showing a different feeling.
tip: When a character reacts differently from others, the author is showing a different point of view.

stem: The story is told from the outside (third person). How would the ending change if Omar told it?
options / answer: A) Maya would no longer be in the story. | B) The bridge would break at the contest. | C) We would hear Omar’s own thoughts about helping his sister. | D) We would learn the name of Maya’s teacher.
why correct: A first-person narrator shares his own thoughts and feelings, so we would know how Omar felt.
tip: Point of view decides whose thoughts the reader can hear.

stem: Which words help you picture the bridge breaking?
options / answer: A) “the class bridge contest” | B) “forty craft sticks” | C) “Next time” | D) “a sharp snap” and “sagged down to the table”
why correct: The sound of a snap and the image of the middle sagging help you see and hear the break.
tip: To visualize, look for words that appeal to your senses.

stem: In the flashback, the sea “looked like a sheet of blue glass.” What should you picture?
options / answer: A) A calm, smooth, shining sea | B) A sea full of big crashing waves | C) A dark, stormy sea | D) A broken window
why correct: A sheet of glass is flat and shiny, so the sea looked calm and smooth.
tip: Comparisons help you build a picture in your mind.

stem: At the end, the boat becomes “only a speck on the bright water.” What does this help you see?
options / answer: A) The boat is very large. | B) The boat is very far away. | C) The water is dark and dirty. | D) The boat is sinking.
why correct: A speck is a tiny dot, so the boat has sailed so far that it looks tiny.
tip: Think about how things look smaller when they are far away.

stem: In “Rain on the Roof,” the words “splashing puddles on the grass” help you picture the rain.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: You can see and hear the water splashing into puddles.
tip: Words that show action and sound help you visualize.

stem: Which line from “Rain on the Roof” helps you HEAR the rain?
options / answer: A) “Slow and low, the gray clouds go” | B) “rolling over the road below” | C) “tapping tin roofs with tiny pins” | D) “Then the sun slides out to say”
why correct: Tapping on tin makes a sound, so this line helps you hear the rain.
tip: Visualizing uses all your senses: sight, sound, touch, smell and taste.

stem: What picture do the last two lines of the poem create?
options / answer: A) Silver coins fall from the sky. | B) The night sky fills with stars. | C) A thunderstorm starts. | D) The rain stops and the sunshine returns.
why correct: The sun “slides out” and tells the showers to “slip away,” so the rain ends.
tip: Picture what the words describe, not their literal meaning.

stem: How is most of “How Honeybees Share Directions” organized?
options / answer: A) It describes how bees use dances to share information. | B) It tells events in time order from one bee’s life. | C) It compares bees with ants. | D) It explains a problem and its solution.
why correct: The article gives details about what the waggle dance and round dance are and what they show.
tip: A description structure gives details and features about one topic.

stem: Which detail describes the waggle dance?
options / answer: A) Bees need food to survive. | B) The bee walks in a straight line while shaking her body. | C) Bees live in colonies. | D) Scientists watched hives with glass walls.
why correct: The second paragraph tells exactly what the dance looks like.
tip: Descriptive details tell what something looks like or how it works.

stem: A text with a description structure gives many details about one topic.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Description gives features, characteristics and examples of a topic.
tip: Signal words for description include “for example,” “such as” and “looks like.”

stem: What does the round dance tell other bees?
options / answer: A) It is time to sleep. | B) The food is very far away. | C) The food is very close to the hive. | D) The hive is in danger.
why correct: The article says the round dance is used when flowers “are very close to the hive.”
tip: Find the paragraph that describes the round dance.

stem: Match each bee movement with what it tells other bees.
options / answer: Direction of the straight line = Which way to fly | Length of the waggle = How far away the food is | Small circles (round dance) = The food is nearby
why correct: The article describes what each part of the dances means.
tip: In a description, each detail explains one feature of the topic.

stem: Why did the author describe the dances in so much detail?
options / answer: A) To explain how to build a beehive. | B) To convince readers to buy honey. | C) To tell a story about one famous bee. | D) To help readers understand how bees communicate without words.
why correct: The details explain how direction and distance are shared through movement.
tip: Authors use description to help readers picture and understand a topic.

stem: Which is the BEST summary of “The Dripping Taps”?
options / answer: A) Students found that taps wasted water, got them fixed, and helped the school save water. | B) Students like making bright signs. | C) A cup was placed under a tap for one hour. | D) Mrs. Hassan is the principal of Al-Noor Elementary.
why correct: A summary tells the most important ideas from beginning to end in a few words.
tip: Include the main problem, the key actions and the result. Leave out small details.

passage: Baking Bread in a Clay Oven
stem: Which detail is LEAST important to include in a summary of “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven”?
options / answer: A) The bread is baked on the hot wall of the oven. | B) The baker uses a padded cushion. | C) The oven is heated with a fire. | D) The dough must rise before baking.
why correct: The cushion is a small detail; the main steps are mixing, rising, heating, shaping and baking.
tip: Summaries keep main ideas and drop small details.

stem: A good summary includes your own opinion about the text.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: A summary retells the important ideas in your own words, without adding opinions.
tip: Summaries are short, accurate and objective.

stem: Which sentence BEST summarizes “The Stick Bridge”?
options / answer: A) Maya has forty craft sticks and a dictionary. | B) Omar likes math books with pictures. | C) When Maya’s bridge breaks, she and Omar fix it with triangles, and it holds at the contest. | D) The bridge contest happens every year.
why correct: This sentence includes the problem, the solution and the result.
tip: A story summary includes the main character, the problem and how it is solved.

stem: Put these sentences in order to make a summary of “How Honeybees Share Directions.”
options / answer: Bees that find food return to the hive. → They dance to show other bees where the food is. → A waggle dance shows direction and distance; a round dance shows food is close. → Scientists learned this by watching hives with glass walls.
why correct: These sentences follow the article from finding food to how scientists learned about the dances.
tip: A summary follows the order of the main ideas in the text.

stem: A student wrote: “The fourth graders measured, wrote, fixed, signed, checked and saved.” What is wrong with this summary?
options / answer: A) It is too long. | B) It uses words from the text. | C) It includes the student’s opinion. | D) It lists actions but does not explain the problem or why it mattered.
why correct: A useful summary explains the main problem (wasted water) and the result (saving water), not just a list of verbs.
tip: Check that a summary would make sense to someone who has not read the text.

stem: Which question is answered in the third paragraph of “How Honeybees Share Directions”?
options / answer: A) How do bees show how far away the food is? | B) What color are honeybees? | C) How do beekeepers collect honey? | D) Why do bees live in colonies?
why correct: The third paragraph says the length of the waggle shows how far away the flowers are.
tip: Match the question to the paragraph that gives the answer.

stem: Which question can you answer using “The Dripping Taps”?
options / answer: A) What is the principal’s favorite subject? | B) What did the class do first to solve the problem? | C) How much did the plumber charge? | D) How many students go to Al-Noor Elementary?
why correct: The text says, “First, the students wrote a letter to the principal.”
tip: Good readers ask questions the text can answer, and find the evidence.

stem: “The Dripping Taps” tells how full the cup was after one hour.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The text says that “By the end of the hour, the cup was almost full.”
tip: Find the exact sentence that answers the question.

stem: A reader asks, “How did scientists learn about the bee dances?” Which sentence answers this question?
options / answer: A) A longer waggle means the food is farther away. | B) She moves in small circles. | C) Scientists learned about these dances by watching bees in hives with glass walls. | D) Honeybees live and work together in large groups called colonies.
why correct: This sentence directly names how scientists studied the bees.
tip: Use key words from the question (scientists, learn) to find the answer.

passage: Baking Bread in a Clay Oven
stem: Which question would be the MOST useful to ask before reading “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven”?
options / answer: A) Who wrote this article? | B) Is the oven red? | C) Do I like bread? | D) What steps are needed to bake bread in a clay oven?
why correct: The title tells you the article explains a process, so asking about the steps guides your reading.
tip: Use the title and headings to ask questions that guide your reading.

stem: Which question CANNOT be answered from “Keeping Bees in the Mountains”?
options / answer: A) How many beekeepers live in the mountains? | B) Where is the honey sold? | C) Why do beekeepers use smoke? | D) Why do beekeepers move their hives?
why correct: The article never gives the number of beekeepers.
tip: Some questions need another source. Check whether the text really gives the answer.

stem: You are not sure what the round dance means. What should you do?
options / answer: A) Skip to the end of the article. | B) Reread the paragraph about the round dance. | C) Guess and keep reading. | D) Read only the title again.
why correct: Rereading the part that explains the round dance will clear up the confusion.
tip: When something is confusing, go back and reread that part slowly.

stem: Rereading can help you find details you missed the first time.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Good readers reread to check their understanding and find evidence.
tip: Rereading is a fix-up strategy, not a sign of a weak reader.

stem: After reading “The Dripping Taps,” you are not sure why the bill was lower. Which part should you reread?
options / answer: A) The paragraph about the letter | B) The title | C) The paragraph about what happened a month later | D) The first sentence only
why correct: The paragraph about checking a month later explains the fixed taps and the lower bill.
tip: Reread the part of the text that matches your question.

passage: Baking Bread in a Clay Oven
stem: Rereading the second paragraph of “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven” helps you answer which question?
options / answer: A) Where is the bread stacked? | B) What is the oven made of? | C) How is the bread taken off the wall? | D) How long does the dough rest?
why correct: The second paragraph says the dough rests “for about an hour.”
tip: Know which paragraph covers which idea before you reread.

stem: Why might a reader reread the sentence “The length of time she waggles tells them how far away the flowers are”?
options / answer: A) To understand how the dance shows distance | B) To find out what honey tastes like | C) To learn the bee’s name | D) To count the paragraphs
why correct: The sentence explains a key idea (distance), so rereading helps you understand it.
tip: Reread sentences that hold important or difficult ideas.

stem: Which TWO are good reasons to reread a text?
options / answer: A) To finish faster | B) To find evidence for an answer | C) To clear up a confusing part | D) To skip the hard words
why correct: Readers reread to check understanding and to find evidence.
tip: Rereading is a tool for understanding.

passage: Baking Bread in a Clay Oven
stem: Put the bread-making steps in order.
options / answer: Mix flour, water, salt and yeast. → Let the dough rise under a cloth. → Press the dough onto the hot oven wall. → Take the bread off with a long hook.
why correct: The article describes mixing, rising, baking and removing, in that order.
tip: Signal words like “early,” “next” and “finally” show the order of steps.

passage: Baking Bread in a Clay Oven
stem: What does the baker do WHILE the dough is rising?
options / answer: A) Presses dough onto the wall | B) Lights a fire inside the oven | C) Takes the bread out of the oven | D) Stacks bread in a basket
why correct: The article says, “While the dough rises, the baker lights a fire inside the oven.”
tip: “While” means two things happen at the same time.

stem: Which word in “The Dripping Taps” signals the second step the class took?
options / answer: A) Later | B) Then | C) Next | D) First
why correct: First they wrote a letter; next the plumber fixed the taps; then they made signs.
tip: Sequence words: first, next, then, after that, finally.

stem: Put the events of “The Dripping Taps” in time order.
options / answer: Students notice dripping taps. → They measure water with a cup. → They write to the principal. → A plumber fixes the taps. → They check again a month later.
why correct: The article tells the events in the order they happened.
tip: Follow time words and the order of paragraphs.

passage: Baking Bread in a Clay Oven
stem: Why is a sequence structure a good choice for “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven”?
options / answer: A) It compares two kinds of bread. | B) It argues that bread is healthy. | C) It tells a story with characters. | D) Making bread is a process that must be done in a certain order.
why correct: Each step depends on the one before it, so time order helps readers follow the process.
tip: Authors choose sequence for processes, instructions and events over time.

passage: Baking Bread in a Clay Oven
stem: What would MOST likely happen if the baker skipped heating the oven?
options / answer: A) The bread would not bake properly on the cool walls. | B) The dough would rise faster. | C) The bread would turn golden more quickly. | D) The bread would not need to be shaped.
why correct: The bread bakes on the “hot inner wall,” so a cool oven would not cook it.
tip: In a process, each step has a reason. Think about why a step is needed.

stem: What problem did the fourth graders find?
options / answer: A) The principal was not at school. | B) Water was being wasted at the school sinks. | C) The cup was too small. | D) The school had no sinks.
why correct: Taps dripped all day and some students left the water running.
tip: In a problem-and-solution text, the problem usually comes first.

stem: Which was one solution to the problem?
options / answer: A) The cup was almost full. | B) The taps dripped all day. | C) A plumber fixed the leaking taps. | D) The students measured water in a cup.
why correct: Fixing the taps stopped the dripping, which solved part of the problem.
tip: A solution is an action that fixes the problem.

stem: In “The Dripping Taps,” making signs was part of the solution.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The signs reminded students to turn off the tap while soaping.
tip: Some problems need more than one solution.

stem: How do you know the solutions worked?
options / answer: A) The signs were bright. | B) The students wrote a letter. | C) The cup was almost full. | D) The taps stopped dripping and the water bill was lower.
why correct: The results a month later show the problem had been solved.
tip: Look for results or evidence after the solution.

stem: Match each problem with the solution the class used.
options / answer: Taps dripped all day = A plumber fixed the taps | Students left water running = Signs reminded them to turn off the tap | The principal did not know = Students wrote her a letter
why correct: Each action answers a different part of the problem.
tip: Match each solution to the part of the problem it fixes.

stem: Why did the author include the detail about the cup of water?
options / answer: A) To show that the problem was real and could be measured | B) To describe the school’s kitchen | C) To explain how to drink more water | D) To show that cups are useful
why correct: The nearly full cup gave the class proof they could share with the principal.
tip: Evidence in a problem-and-solution text shows how serious the problem is.

stem: Which group of words from “Rain on the Roof” shows alliteration?
options / answer: A) window, glass, drip | B) tapping, tin, tiny | C) clouds, gray, low | D) splashing, puddles, grass
why correct: “Tapping,” “tin” and “tiny” all begin with the same t sound.
tip: Alliteration is the repetition of the same beginning sound in nearby words.

stem: Which line repeats the long o sound (assonance)?
options / answer: A) “Drip and drop on the window glass,” | B) “Pitter, patter, the rain begins,” | C) “Slow and low, the gray clouds go,” | D) “splashing puddles on the grass.”
why correct: “Slow,” “low” and “go” share the long o vowel sound.
tip: Assonance is the repetition of vowel sounds in nearby words.

stem: In “Silver showers, slip away,” the s sound is repeated.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: “Silver,” “showers” and “slip” begin with s sounds, which is alliteration.
tip: Say the words aloud to hear repeated sounds.

stem: Match each sound device with its example from the poem.
options / answer: Alliteration = tapping tin roofs with tiny pins | Assonance = Slow and low, the gray clouds go | Onomatopoeia = Pitter, patter
why correct: Repeated beginning sounds, repeated vowel sounds, and words that imitate sounds.
tip: Say each line aloud and listen for which sounds repeat.

stem: Why does the poet repeat sounds in “Drip and drop”?
options / answer: A) To make the poem longer | B) To explain where rain comes from | C) To show that the rain is dangerous | D) To imitate the sound of rain falling
why correct: The short, repeated d sounds feel like drops hitting the glass.
tip: Poets use sound devices to help readers hear and feel what is described.

stem: Which sentence uses consonance (a repeated consonant sound inside or at the end of words)?
options / answer: A) The black cat sat back on the mat. | B) The bee sees three trees. | C) Bright blue birds bounced by. | D) Buzz went the busy bee.
why correct: The t sound repeats at the end of “cat,” “sat” and “mat,” and the k sound in “black” and “back.”
tip: Consonance repeats consonant sounds that are not only at the beginning of words.

stem: What topic do “How Honeybees Share Directions” and “Keeping Bees in the Mountains” have in common?
options / answer: A) Clay ovens | B) Honeybees | C) Pearl diving | D) School water use
why correct: Both texts give information about honeybees.
tip: First find what two texts share, then look for differences.

stem: How is the focus of the two bee texts different?
options / answer: A) Both tell a story about one beekeeper. | B) Both explain only how honey tastes. | C) One explains bee dances; the other explains how people keep bees. | D) One is about ants and one is about bees.
why correct: “How Honeybees Share Directions” is about dances; “Keeping Bees in the Mountains” is about beekeepers.
tip: Compare the main idea of each text.

stem: Both bee texts say that bees need flowers to find food.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: One describes bees dancing to show where flowers are; the other says bees near many flowers fly less far.
tip: Look for a key idea that appears in both texts.

stem: Using BOTH texts, why might beekeepers move hives near blooming flowers?
options / answer: A) Because flowers keep bees warm at night. | B) Because honey is sold near flowers. | C) Because bees cannot dance near flowers. | D) So bees do not need to fly far, and dancing bees can lead others to food nearby.
why correct: Text 2 explains that nearby flowers mean shorter flights; Text 1 shows that bees share where nearby food is.
tip: Combine information from both texts to answer a bigger question.

stem: Which TWO details come ONLY from “Keeping Bees in the Mountains”?
options / answer: A) Beekeepers use gentle smoke to calm bees. | B) Scientists watched hives with glass walls. | C) A longer waggle means the food is farther away. | D) Honey from the mountains is sold at local markets.
why correct: The smoke and the markets are only described in the mountain beekeeping text.
tip: Keep track of which text each detail comes from.

stem: A student wants to write a report on how bees and people work together. Which text is MORE useful, and why?
options / answer: A) “Keeping Bees in the Mountains,” because it explains how beekeepers care for bees and collect honey. | B) Neither text, because both are only about flowers. | C) “The Dripping Taps,” because it is about saving water. | D) “How Honeybees Share Directions,” because it explains bee dances.
why correct: The mountain text describes what beekeepers do: moving hives, calming bees, and leaving honey.
tip: Choose the source that best matches the research question.

stem: What is the complete subject? “The tall giraffe ate leaves from the tree.”
options / answer: A) ate leaves from the tree | B) The tall giraffe | C) the tree | D) leaves
why correct: The complete subject tells who or what the sentence is about: the tall giraffe.
tip: Ask: Who or what is the sentence about?

stem: What is the simple subject? “My older cousin from Jeddah visited us on Friday.”
options / answer: A) Jeddah | B) visited | C) cousin | D) older
why correct: The simple subject is the main noun in the complete subject: cousin.
tip: Remove the describing words; the main noun that is left is the simple subject.

stem: What is the simple predicate? “The students in Room 4 planted seeds in the garden.”
options / answer: A) seeds | B) in the garden | C) students | D) planted
why correct: The simple predicate is the main verb that tells what the subject did.
tip: Find the main action word in the predicate.

stem: In “Lina and Sara painted a mural,” the sentence has a compound subject.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Two subjects, Lina and Sara, share the same predicate, joined by “and.”
tip: A compound subject is two or more subjects with the same predicate.

stem: Which sentence has a compound predicate?
options / answer: A) Ahmed washed the dishes and dried them. | B) The clean dishes were on the shelf. | C) Ahmed washed the dishes quickly. | D) Ahmed and Ali washed the dishes.
why correct: “Washed the dishes” and “dried them” are two predicates for the same subject.
tip: A compound predicate has two or more verbs for one subject, usually joined by and or or.

stem: Add a predicate to make a complete sentence: “The noisy crowd ____ when the team scored.”
options / answer: (typed)
correct: cheered / clapped / shouted / roared / yelled / jumped / celebrated / screamed
why correct: A predicate tells what the subject did, such as “cheered.”
tip: Every complete sentence needs a subject and a predicate.

stem: Which group of words is an independent clause?
options / answer: A) Because the bus arrived late | B) The bus arrived late. | C) When the bus arrived | D) After the late bus
why correct: An independent clause has a subject and a verb and can stand alone as a sentence.
tip: Read it alone. If it makes a complete thought, it is independent.

stem: Which word begins the dependent clause? “We stayed inside because it was very windy.”
options / answer: A) inside | B) We | C) because | D) windy
why correct: “Because it was very windy” is a dependent clause that begins with the subordinating conjunction “because.”
tip: Dependent clauses often begin with because, when, before, after, if or although.

stem: “When the bell rings” can stand alone as a complete sentence.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: It is a dependent clause; it leaves the reader asking, “What happens when the bell rings?”
tip: A dependent clause cannot stand alone as a sentence.

stem: Which sentence is a complex sentence?
options / answer: A) We ate lunch, and we played football. | B) We ate lunch and played football. | C) We ate lunch. | D) After we ate lunch, we played football.
why correct: A complex sentence has an independent clause and at least one dependent clause (“After we ate lunch”).
tip: Look for a subordinating conjunction such as after, when or because.

stem: Choose the best subordinating conjunction: “____ it rained all morning, the picnic went ahead in the afternoon.”
options / answer: A) Although | B) Until | C) Because | D) And
why correct: “Although” shows a contrast: rain in the morning, but the picnic still happened.
tip: Choose the conjunction that shows the right relationship between ideas.

stem: Match each dependent clause with the main clause that completes it best.
options / answer: Before you cross the street, = look both ways. | Because the oven was hot, = the bread baked quickly. | If you finish early, = you may read a book.
why correct: Each dependent clause needs a main clause that completes the thought logically.
tip: Read each pair as one sentence to check that it makes sense.

stem: Which sentence is a compound sentence?
options / answer: A) I wanted to swim, but the pool was closed. | B) The pool and the gym were closed. | C) Because the pool was closed, I went home. | D) I wanted to swim in the pool.
why correct: It has two independent clauses joined by a comma and “but.”
tip: A compound sentence joins two complete sentences with a coordinating conjunction.

stem: Where does the comma belong? “Huda read a book and her sister drew a picture.”
options / answer: A) No comma is needed | B) After “book,” before “and” | C) After “sister” | D) After “Huda”
why correct: Use a comma before the coordinating conjunction when it joins two independent clauses.
tip: Put the comma just before and, but or or when each part could be its own sentence.

stem: Choose the conjunction: “Do you want rice ____ do you want bread?”
options / answer: A) so | B) or | C) because | D) but
why correct: “Or” shows a choice between two options.
tip: and = adds, but = contrasts, or = gives a choice, so = shows a result.

stem: Choose the conjunction: “The road was icy, ____ the drivers went slowly.”
options / answer: A) or | B) but | C) so | D) nor
why correct: The drivers went slowly as a result of the icy road, so “so” fits.
tip: Ask how the two ideas are related: result, contrast, choice or addition.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The sun set |  and |  the stars came out |  slowly.
why correct: A comma is needed before “and” because it joins two independent clauses.
tip: Check whether both parts could stand alone as sentences.

stem: Which is the best way to combine these sentences? “Nasser likes math. He does not like spelling.”
options / answer: A) Nasser likes math, and he does not like spelling. | B) Nasser likes math he does not like spelling. | C) Nasser likes math, but he does not like spelling. | D) Nasser likes math, so he does not like spelling.
why correct: The ideas contrast, so a comma and “but” join them correctly.
tip: Choose the conjunction that matches the relationship between the ideas.

stem: Combine the sentences: “Jamal washes the dishes. Teri washes the dishes.”
options / answer: A) Jamal washes and Teri washes the dishes. | B) Jamal and Teri washes the dishes. | C) Jamal washes the dishes Teri. | D) Jamal and Teri wash the dishes.
why correct: Join the two subjects with “and,” remove repeated words, and make the verb agree: wash.
tip: When you combine subjects, check that the verb agrees with the new plural subject.

stem: Combine the sentences: “Our team won the game. Our team won the trophy.”
options / answer: A) Our team won the game and the trophy. | B) The game and the trophy won our team. | C) Our team won and our team won. | D) Our team won the game our team won the trophy.
why correct: Join the two objects with “and” and leave out the repeated words “Our team won.”
tip: Leave out words that repeat when you combine sentences.

stem: “Mona sings. Mona dances.” can be combined as “Mona sings and dances.”
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The two predicates share one subject, so they can be joined with “and.”
tip: If two sentences have the same subject, you can join their predicates.

stem: Combine the sentences using an appositive: “Mr. Salem teaches science. Mr. Salem is our neighbor.”
options / answer: A) Our neighbor teaches Mr. Salem science. | B) Mr. Salem, our neighbor, teaches science. | C) Mr. Salem our neighbor teaches science. | D) Mr. Salem teaches science our neighbor.
why correct: An appositive renames a noun and is set off with commas: “our neighbor.”
tip: Place the appositive right after the noun it renames, with commas around it.

stem: Which is the BEST combined sentence? “The kite was red. The kite was huge. The kite flew over the park.”
options / answer: A) Over the park the red the huge kite flew. | B) The kite was red, huge, flew over the park. | C) The huge red kite flew over the park. | D) The kite was red and the kite was huge and the kite flew over the park.
why correct: Move the describing words before the noun and keep one predicate.
tip: Adjectives from short sentences can often move in front of the noun.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: Fatima and her brother |  plays |  chess |  every evening.
why correct: A compound subject joined by “and” is plural, so the verb must be “play.”
tip: After combining subjects, check subject-verb agreement.

stem: Choose the correct word: “The ____ tail was long and fluffy.”
options / answer: A) cat | B) cats | C) cats’ | D) cat’s
why correct: One cat owns the tail, so add an apostrophe and s: cat’s.
tip: Singular possessive: add ’s.

stem: Choose the correct word: “The two ____ bikes were in the garage.”
options / answer: A) boys’ | B) boys | C) boy’s | D) boyses
why correct: Plural nouns that end in s take only an apostrophe: boys’.
tip: Plural possessive ending in s: add only ’.

stem: Choose the correct word: “The ____ coats hung by the door.”
options / answer: A) childrens’ | B) children’s | C) childs’ | D) children
why correct: For plural nouns that do not end in s, add an apostrophe and s: children’s.
tip: Irregular plurals (men, women, children, people) take ’s.

stem: Which sentence uses a possessive noun correctly?
options / answer: A) The teacher’s were busy all day. | B) The teachers’s desk was covered with papers. | C) The teachers desk was covered with papers. | D) The teacher’s desk was covered with papers.
why correct: One teacher owns the desk, so “teacher’s” is correct.
tip: Ask: Does the word show ownership? Is the owner singular or plural?

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The three girls’ |  team won |  the schools |  trophy.
why correct: The trophy belongs to the school, so “school’s” needs an apostrophe and s.
tip: Check every noun that comes right before something it owns.

stem: Match each phrase with its correct possessive form.
options / answer: the toy of the dog = the dog’s toy | the toys of the dogs = the dogs’ toys | the hats of the women = the women’s hats
why correct: One dog: ’s. Two dogs: s’. Women (plural without s): ’s.
tip: Decide singular or plural first, then whether the plural ends in s.

stem: Choose the contraction for “do not”: “I ____ like cold soup.”
options / answer: A) doesn’t | B) do’nt | C) don’t | D) dont
why correct: An apostrophe replaces the missing o: do not → don’t.
tip: In a contraction, the apostrophe takes the place of missing letters.

stem: Write the contraction for “it is”: “____ time to go home.”
options / answer: (typed)
why correct: It is → it’s. The apostrophe replaces the i in “is.”
tip: Say both words quickly to hear the contraction.

stem: Choose the correct word: “The bird fed ____ babies.”
options / answer: A) its’ | B) it’s | C) it is | D) its
why correct: “Its” is a possessive pronoun, and possessive pronouns do not have apostrophes.
tip: Try “it is.” If it does not make sense, use “its.”

stem: Which sentence uses an apostrophe correctly?
options / answer: A) They’re going to the museum today. | B) Their going to the museum today. | C) The cat licked it’s paw. | D) The book is your’s.
why correct: “They’re” is the contraction of “they are,” which fits the sentence.
tip: Expand the contraction to check if it makes sense.

stem: Match each contraction with the words it stands for.
options / answer: we’ll = we will | wouldn’t = would not | she’s = she is | they’ve = they have
why correct: Each apostrophe replaces the missing letters in the second word.
tip: Say the two words slowly, then quickly, to match the contraction.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: Its’ |  a shame that |  the dog hurt |  its leg.
why correct: The first word should be “It’s,” meaning “It is.” The second “its” is correct because it shows ownership.
tip: “It’s” = it is. “Its” = belonging to it. “Its’” is never correct.

stem: Which is the correct abbreviation for “Doctor”?
options / answer: A) DR | B) Dr. | C) dr | D) Dtr.
why correct: The title Doctor is abbreviated “Dr.” with a capital D and a period.
tip: Titles before names (Mr., Mrs., Dr.) begin with a capital and end with a period.

stem: Which title of a story is written correctly?
options / answer: A) “the Lost Kite” | B) the lost kite | C) “The Lost Kite” | D) “The lost Kite”
why correct: Story titles go in quotation marks, and the first word and important words are capitalized.
tip: Use quotation marks for stories, poems, songs and articles.

stem: The title of a book should be underlined or written in italics.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Long works such as books, movies and magazines are underlined or italicized.
tip: Short works go in quotation marks; long works are italicized or underlined.

stem: Nadia recited a poem called desert moon at the assembly. How should the poem’s title be written?
options / answer: A) Desert Moon (with no marks) | B) ‘Desert Moon’ | C) “desert moon” | D) “Desert Moon”
why correct: Poem titles go in quotation marks, with the first word and important words capitalized.
tip: Short works (poems, songs, stories, articles) take quotation marks.

stem: Which is the correct greeting for a friendly letter?
options / answer: A) Dear Aunt Mariam, | B) Dear aunt mariam, | C) Dear Aunt Mariam. | D) dear Aunt Mariam,
why correct: Capitalize the first word and the name, and end the greeting with a comma.
tip: Friendly letter: greeting with a comma; closing such as “Your friend,” with a comma.

stem: Put the parts of a friendly letter in order.
options / answer: Date → Greeting (Dear Huda,) → Body → Closing (Your friend,) → Signature
why correct: A friendly letter has five parts in this order.
tip: Remember: date, greeting, body, closing, signature.

stem: Which word has the most positive connotation?
options / answer: A) thin | B) slender | C) bony | D) skinny
why correct: All four words mean “not heavy,” but “slender” suggests something graceful and pleasant.
tip: Connotation is the feeling a word gives, beyond its dictionary meaning.

stem: Which word gives a more negative feeling? “The old house was ____.”
options / answer: A) cozy | B) charming | C) creepy | D) quiet
why correct: “Creepy” suggests fear, which is a negative feeling.
tip: Think about how the word makes you feel.

stem: “Home” and “house” have the same denotation but different connotations.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Both name a building where people live, but “home” suggests warmth and family.
tip: Denotation = dictionary meaning. Connotation = feeling.

stem: A writer wants readers to admire a boy who asks many questions. Which word should describe him?
options / answer: A) rude | B) nosy | C) pushy | D) curious
why correct: “Curious” shows a positive love of learning, while the others sound negative.
tip: Writers choose words with connotations that match the feeling they want.

stem: Match each neutral word with a word that has a more positive connotation.
options / answer: cheap = affordable | talkative = chatty | old = antique | smell = scent
why correct: Each pair has a similar meaning, but the second word sounds more pleasant.
tip: Ask which word you would rather hear about yourself or your things.

stem: In a poem, the moon “crept” over the hills instead of “rose.” What feeling does “crept” add?
options / answer: A) A slow, quiet, slightly mysterious feeling | B) No feeling; it means exactly the same as “rose” | C) A fast and noisy feeling | D) A happy, sunny feeling
why correct: “Crept” suggests slow, quiet movement, which adds mystery to the scene.
tip: Compare the feeling of the author’s word with a plain word.

stem: Choose the correct word: “We ate dinner at ____ house.”
options / answer: A) their | B) there | C) they’re | D) thier
why correct: “Their” shows ownership: the house belongs to them.
tip: their = belongs to them; there = a place; they’re = they are.

stem: Choose the correct word: “I can ____ the birds singing.”
options / answer: A) heer | B) hear | C) hair | D) here
why correct: “Hear” is what you do with your ears.
tip: Hear has the word ear inside it.

stem: Which pair of words are homophones?
options / answer: A) hot / cold | B) flower / flour | C) big / large | D) bat / bat
why correct: Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings.
tip: Homo = same, phone = sound.

stem: In which sentence does “bow” mean to bend forward?
options / answer: A) He shot an arrow with a bow. | B) The bow of the ship cut through the waves. | C) The actors bow at the end of the play. | D) She tied a bow in her hair.
why correct: Actors bend forward to thank the audience, so “bow” means to bend.
tip: Homographs are spelled the same but have different meanings. Use context clues.

stem: Read: “The wind was too strong, so we had to wind the kite string back in.” How are the two words pronounced?
options / answer: A) Both rhyme with “pinned” | B) The same in both places | C) Both rhyme with “find” | D) Differently: wind (moving air) and wind (to turn)
why correct: The first “wind” rhymes with “pinned”; the second rhymes with “find.” They are homographs.
tip: Some homographs change pronunciation as well as meaning.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The wind blew |  threw the open window |  and knocked |  over the vase.
why correct: “Through” means in one side and out the other. “Threw” is the past tense of “throw.”
tip: Homophones sound the same, so check the meaning of each spelling.

stem: Where would you look to find a synonym for “happy”?
options / answer: A) A thesaurus | B) A calendar | C) An atlas | D) A glossary
why correct: A thesaurus lists synonyms and antonyms.
tip: Thesaurus = words with similar meanings.

stem: What does a glossary contain?
options / answer: A) A list of chapters and page numbers | B) Meanings of important words used in that book | C) Maps of different countries | D) Synonyms for every word in English
why correct: A glossary is a small dictionary at the back of a book for words used in that book.
tip: Glossaries are in the back of nonfiction books and textbooks.

stem: A dictionary can show how to pronounce a word.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Dictionary entries give pronunciation, syllables, meanings and parts of speech.
tip: Look for the respelling in parentheses after the entry word.

stem: Guide words at the top of a dictionary page are “mango” and “market.” Which word would be on that page?
options / answer: A) magic | B) melon | C) map | D) mask
why correct: “Map” comes after “mango” (n before p) and before “market” (p before r).
tip: Guide words show the first and last words on the page. Use ABC order.

stem: A dictionary entry says: “bat (noun) 1. a club used to hit a ball 2. a flying animal.” Which meaning fits “The bat hung upside down in the cave”?
options / answer: A) Neither meaning | B) Meaning 1 | C) Both meanings | D) Meaning 2
why correct: Animals hang upside down in caves, so the second meaning fits.
tip: Read each meaning and test it in the sentence.

stem: Put these words in the order they would appear in a dictionary.
options / answer: camel → camera → camp → canal → candle
why correct: Compare letters one by one: cam-e-l, cam-e-r, cam-p, can-a, can-d.
tip: When the first letters match, compare the next letter.

stem: What is the main conflict in “The Last Repair”?
options / answer: A) Khalid must fix the captain’s watch before the ship sails, but he loses the spring. | B) Khalid and his uncle argue about the shop. | C) Khalid wants to become a sailor. | D) The captain refuses to pay for the repair.
why correct: Khalid faces a deadline (sunset) and a sudden problem (the missing spring).
tip: The conflict is the main problem that creates tension in a story.

stem: What kind of conflict does Khalid face when his hands shake and the spring flies away?
options / answer: A) A conflict with nature | B) A conflict with himself (his nerves) | C) A conflict with society | D) A conflict with another character
why correct: His shaking hands and pounding heart show that the struggle is inside him.
tip: Conflicts can be with another character, nature, society or oneself.

stem: How does Khalid resolve the conflict?
options / answer: A) He waits for Uncle Faris to get well. | B) He gives the captain a different watch. | C) He calms himself, searches slowly, and finds the spring in his apron. | D) He buys a new spring from another shop.
why correct: He counts to ten, uses the magnifying glass, and finds the spring caught in his apron.
tip: Look at what the character does differently to solve the problem.

stem: In “The Two Wells,” the conflict begins when Hamdan builds a wall around the well.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Charging for water makes the poorest families go thirsty, which creates the problem.
tip: The conflict usually begins with an event that changes everyday life.

stem: How does the resolution of “The Two Wells” change Hamdan?
options / answer: A) He leaves the village forever. | B) He makes the children pay for their well. | C) He builds a second wall around the new well. | D) He realizes sharing is more valuable than selling and opens the gate.
why correct: When no one buys his water, he unlocks the gate and says shared water is worth more.
tip: A strong resolution often shows how a character has changed.

stem: Which detail BEST shows that the conflict in “The Two Wells” affects the whole village, not just Salma?
options / answer: A) “The poorest families began to go thirsty.” | B) “Hamdan laughed at them from his gate.” | C) “Salma watched the palm trees outside the village.” | D) “Their hands blistered.”
why correct: Many families suffer when water is sold, so the conflict reaches the whole community.
tip: Look for details that show who is affected by a problem.

stem: Put the main events of “The Last Repair” in order.
options / answer: The captain leaves his watch at the shop. → Khalid cleans every gear. → The spring flies away. → Khalid finds the spring in his apron. → The watch ticks as the ship’s horn sounds.
why correct: The events follow the afternoon from the captain’s visit to the ship’s departure.
tip: Plot events build toward a climax and then a resolution.

stem: What is the climax of “The Last Repair”?
options / answer: A) The captain leaves the watch in the morning. | B) Khalid finds the spring and the watch ticks as the horn sounds. | C) Khalid runs to the dock. | D) Khalid cleans the gears.
why correct: The moment of greatest tension is solved when the watch starts ticking just in time.
tip: The climax is the turning point, where the tension is highest.

stem: Which event causes Khalid to knock the box of screws to the floor?
options / answer: A) His uncle calls him from the other room. | B) The ship’s horn startles him. | C) He panics after the spring disappears. | D) The captain returns early.
why correct: After the spring vanishes, Khalid sweeps his hands across the bench in panic.
tip: Events in a plot are often connected by cause and effect.

stem: How does the flashback fit into the structure of the plot?
options / answer: A) It has no connection to the main events. | B) It is the resolution of the story. | C) It is the opening event of the story. | D) It interrupts the rising action and gives Khalid the idea that solves the problem.
why correct: Remembering his uncle’s lesson leads Khalid to slow down and find the spring.
tip: Ask how each part of a story helps the plot move forward.

stem: Which TWO events are part of the rising action in “The Two Wells”?
options / answer: A) Hamdan charges a coin for each bucket. | B) The children dig for seven days. | C) The villagers name the Children’s Well. | D) Hamdan unlocks his gate.
why correct: Rising action is the series of events that build tension before the climax.
tip: Rising action comes after the conflict begins and before the turning point.

stem: Why does the author end “The Two Wells” with Hamdan’s words?
options / answer: A) To show the lesson of the story through the character who learned it. | B) To explain where Hamdan’s money came from. | C) To introduce a new problem for the village. | D) To describe how the new well was dug.
why correct: Hamdan’s final line states the theme of sharing, closing the story.
tip: The final event of a folktale often states its lesson.

stem: Which paragraph of “The Last Repair” is a flashback?
options / answer: A) The one about the captain leaving the watch | B) The one about Khalid at age eight and the sand timer | C) The one about the ship’s horn | D) The one about the spring flying away
why correct: The story goes back to “the first day his uncle had let him touch a watch,” when he was eight.
tip: A flashback moves back in time to an earlier event.

stem: Which words signal the start of the flashback?
options / answer: A) “There, caught in the folds…” | B) “Now Khalid closed his eyes…” | C) “Then he remembered…” | D) “By late afternoon…”
why correct: The verb “remembered” tells the reader the story is going back in time.
tip: Look for words like remembered, years ago, or had + verb.

stem: What does the flashback reveal about Uncle Faris?
options / answer: A) He wanted Khalid to become a sailor. | B) He does not trust Khalid with watches. | C) He is strict and often angry. | D) He is a patient teacher who helped Khalid stay calm.
why correct: He gently teaches that a watchmaker’s hands must be slower than the sand.
tip: Flashbacks often reveal character traits through past events.

stem: The flashback in “The Last Repair” happens before the captain leaves his watch.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The flashback is from when Khalid was eight, years before the day of the story.
tip: Compare the time of the flashback with the time of the main story.

stem: How would the story change if the author removed the flashback?
options / answer: A) Readers would not understand why Khalid suddenly calms down. | B) The captain would not need his watch. | C) The story would happen in a different city. | D) Khalid would not have a problem.
why correct: The memory of the sand timer explains why Khalid counts slowly and searches calmly.
tip: Ask what a flashback explains that the reader would otherwise miss.

stem: The sand timer in the flashback and the ship’s horn at the end are both connected to time. Why does the author include both?
options / answer: A) To prove that sand timers are more accurate than watches | B) To show Khalid learning to work calmly even under time pressure | C) To show that ships always leave late | D) To explain how sand timers are made
why correct: The timer teaches patience; the horn shows the deadline. Together they show Khalid using patience against time.
tip: Look for how details in a flashback connect to the main story.

stem: Where and when does “The Two Wells” take place?
options / answer: A) Today, in a large city | B) On a ship at sea | C) Long ago, in a village at the edge of a desert | D) In a mountain forest
why correct: The first sentence gives both the time (long ago) and the place (a desert village).
tip: Folktales often begin with a time and place like “Long ago, in…”

stem: Why is the desert setting important to the conflict?
options / answer: A) Deserts have many wells, so water is cheap. | B) The desert is too hot for the children to play. | C) The desert makes the merchant rich from gold. | D) In a desert, water is scarce, so controlling the only well gives Hamdan power.
why correct: Because water is rare in a desert, owning the only well lets Hamdan charge for it.
tip: Ask how the place creates or shapes the problem.

stem: Which detail about the setting helps Salma solve the problem?
options / answer: A) One grove of palm trees stays green in the hottest month. | B) Hamdan builds a gate. | C) The village is at the edge of a desert. | D) Every child knows the way to the well in the dark.
why correct: Salma reasons that green trees in the heat mean water is close to the surface.
tip: Setting details can be clues that characters use.

stem: Which details show the time period of “The Last Repair”?
options / answer: A) The fever and the bench | B) The year 1955 and the ship’s captain who needs a pocket watch | C) Khalid’s age and his apron | D) The magnifying glass and the tweezers
why correct: The story names 1955, and a captain depending on a pocket watch fits that time.
tip: Look for dates and objects from a particular period.

stem: The smells of sea salt and cardamom help show that “The Last Repair” is set in a port city.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Sea salt suggests the sea, and the story mentions a harbor and a ship.
tip: Sensory details can show the setting without naming it directly.

stem: How does the setting of the harbor add to the tension at the end of “The Last Repair”?
options / answer: A) The harbor is far away, so the captain cannot be found. | B) The harbor is noisy, so Khalid cannot work. | C) The ship’s horn across the harbor shows that time has run out. | D) The harbor floods the shop.
why correct: The horn is a sound from the setting that signals the deadline, adding urgency.
tip: Setting can add tension through sounds, weather or time.

stem: After Salma notices the green grove, what will she most likely do?
options / answer: A) Cut down the palm trees. | B) Buy water from Hamdan. | C) Move to another village. | D) Look for water near the green trees.
why correct: She says, “Water must be close to the surface there.”
tip: A character’s observations often lead to their next action.

stem: When Hamdan laughs at the children digging, what can readers predict?
options / answer: A) Hamdan will be proven wrong. | B) Hamdan will help them dig. | C) The children will buy Hamdan’s water. | D) The children will stop digging that day.
why correct: In folktales, a character who mocks hard work is often proven wrong.
tip: Use what you know about how folktales usually go.
