tip: The simple subject is never inside a prepositional phrase.

stem: In “Under the old bridge lived a family of ducks,” the subject comes after the verb.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The verb is “lived”; the subject “a family of ducks” comes after it.
tip: In inverted sentences, ask “Who or what lived?” to find the subject.

stem: Which sentence has BOTH a compound subject and a compound predicate?
options / answer: A) Reem wrote the script, and Dana directed the play. | B) Reem and Dana wrote the script and directed the play. | C) Reem and Dana wrote the script. | D) Reem wrote the script and directed the play.
why correct: Two subjects (Reem, Dana) share two predicates (wrote…, directed…).
tip: Find the subjects first, then the verbs.

stem: What is the simple predicate? “The students have been practicing their lines all week.”
options / answer: A) all week | B) their lines | C) have been practicing | D) practicing
why correct: The simple predicate is the whole verb phrase: have been practicing.
tip: Include helping verbs in the simple predicate.

stem: Add a simple subject that makes sense: “At dawn, the hungry ____ chirped loudly in the nest.”
options / answer: (typed)
correct: birds / chicks / sparrows / baby birds / nestlings / bird / chick / robins / pigeons / finches
why correct: Something in a nest that chirps, such as “birds,” is a logical subject.
tip: The subject is who or what does the action.

stem: Which is a run-on sentence?
options / answer: A) I went to the store, but it was closed. | B) When I went to the store. | C) I went to the store. | D) I went to the store it was closed.
why correct: Two complete sentences are joined with no conjunction or punctuation.
tip: A run-on joins sentences without the proper conjunction and punctuation.

stem: Which is a sentence fragment?
options / answer: A) After the long, rainy weekend. | B) We stayed inside all weekend. | C) It rained, so we played games. | D) The weekend was long and rainy.
why correct: It has no subject and verb that complete a thought.
tip: A fragment leaves the reader asking, “What happened?”

stem: Which is the best way to correct this run-on? “The museum was crowded we waited an hour.”
options / answer: A) The museum was crowded, we waited an hour. | B) The museum was crowded, so we waited an hour. | C) The museum was crowded we, waited an hour. | D) The museum crowded we waited.
why correct: A comma plus the conjunction “so” correctly joins the two independent clauses.
tip: Fix run-ons with a period, or a comma plus and/but/or/so.

stem: “Running down the hallway with a heavy backpack” is a complete sentence.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: It has no subject and no complete verb; it is a fragment.
tip: Ask: Who is running? A complete sentence would tell you.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: Our team practiced hard | , we |  won the |  championship.
why correct: A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences; add a conjunction such as “and.”
tip: Two independent clauses need a comma AND a conjunction, or a period.

stem: Which revision fixes BOTH problems? “Because the bus was late. We missed the start of the play we were upset.”
options / answer: A) The bus was late we missed the start. Of the play we were upset. | B) Because the bus was late. We missed the start of the play, we were upset. | C) Because the bus was late, we missed the start of the play. We were upset. | D) Because the bus was late, we missed the start of the play we were upset.
why correct: Attaching the fragment to the next clause and splitting the run-on fixes both errors.
tip: Fix fragments by joining them to a sentence; fix run-ons by separating or properly joining clauses.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: Choose the correct plural: “We packed our ____ for the trip.”
options / answer: A) lunches | B) lunchies | C) lunchs | D) lunch’s
why correct: Add -es to nouns ending in s, sh, ch or x: lunch → lunches.
tip: Words ending in s, sh, ch or x add -es.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: Choose the correct plural: “The library has three ____ of that book.”
options / answer: A) copys | B) copies | C) copy’s | D) copyes
why correct: Copy ends in a consonant + y, so change y to i and add -es: copies.
tip: Vowel + y → add s (keys). Consonant + y → ies (copies).

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: Choose the correct plural: “Autumn ____ covered the path.”
options / answer: A) leafs | B) leafes | C) leaves | D) leave
why correct: Some nouns ending in f change the f to v and add -es: leaf → leaves.
tip: Watch for f/fe words: leaf/leaves, knife/knives, half/halves.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: Which sentence uses an irregular plural correctly?
options / answer: A) My tooths are clean. | B) Three deers drank from the stream. | C) The childs played in the yard. | D) Three deer drank from the stream.
why correct: “Deer” is the same in singular and plural.
tip: Learn irregular plurals: deer, sheep, fish; tooth/teeth; child/children.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: Match each singular noun with its plural.
options / answer: piano = pianos | potato = potatoes | monkey = monkeys | woman = women
why correct: Some -o words add s, others add es; vowel + y adds s; woman is irregular.
tip: Check the letter before the final y or o.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: Which sentence uses a collective noun with the correct verb?
options / answer: A) The orchestra plays every Thursday evening. | B) The orchestra play every Thursday evening. | C) The orchestras plays every Thursday evening. | D) The orchestra are playing every Thursday evening.
why correct: “Orchestra” names one group acting together, so it takes the singular verb “plays.”
tip: Collective nouns (team, class, family) usually take singular verbs.

stem: Choose the correct possessive: “____ bicycle has a flat tire.”
options / answer: A) Lucas | B) Lucases | C) Luca’s | D) Lucas’s
why correct: In your Wonders book, a name ending in s takes an apostrophe and s: Lucas’s.
tip: Names and singular nouns ending in s: add ’s (Lucas’s, the class’s).

stem: Choose the correct possessive: “The ____ final project won first prize.”
options / answer: A) class’s | B) classes’ | C) class | D) classes
why correct: One class owns the project; a singular noun ending in s adds ’s.
tip: Decide whether there is one owner or more than one.

stem: Choose the correct possessive: “The ____ uniforms were washed after the match.”
options / answer: A) athletes | B) athletes’ | C) athlete’s | D) athletes’s
why correct: A plural noun ending in s adds only an apostrophe: athletes’.
tip: Plural ending in s → add only ’.

stem: Which phrase is written correctly?
options / answer: A) the peoples hometown | B) the people’s hometown | C) the peoples’ hometown | D) the people’s’ hometown
why correct: Plural nouns that do not end in s add ’s: people’s.
tip: Irregular plurals (people, women, children, oxen) add ’s.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The two |  authors |  books |  offer clues.
why correct: The books belong to two authors, so the plural possessive is “authors’.”
tip: If a plural noun shows ownership, it needs an apostrophe.

stem: Which sentence correctly uses both a plural noun and a possessive noun?
options / answer: A) The atlases index lists all the island’s. | B) The atlas index list’s all the islands. | C) The atlas’s index lists all the islands. | D) The atla’s index lists all the islands.
why correct: “Atlas’s” is a singular possessive; “islands” is a plain plural.
tip: Do not confuse plurals with possessives.

stem: Choose the contraction for “are not”: “The shops ____ open on Fridays.”
options / answer: A) isn’t | B) are’nt | C) aren’t | D) arent
why correct: are + not → aren’t; the apostrophe replaces the o.
tip: The apostrophe goes where letters are left out.

stem: Choose the correct word: “____ going to love this museum!”
options / answer: A) Youre | B) Your | C) Yours | D) You’re
why correct: You are → you’re. Test it: “You are going to love this museum.”
tip: Your = belongs to you; you’re = you are.

stem: Which word is a modal helping verb in “You should wear a helmet”?
options / answer: A) You | B) wear | C) helmet | D) should
why correct: Modals such as can, could, may, might, must, should and would express possibility or obligation.
tip: A modal comes before the main verb and changes its meaning.

stem: Which modal shows that something is REQUIRED? “Visitors ____ show a ticket at the gate.”
options / answer: A) must | B) might | C) may | D) could
why correct: “Must” expresses obligation.
tip: must = required; may/might = possible; can/could = able.

stem: Choose the correct pronoun: “The twins built the model by ____.”
options / answer: A) themselves | B) themself | C) their’s | D) theirselves
why correct: Plural reflexive pronouns end in -selves: themselves.
tip: -self for one, -selves for more than one.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The company |  lost |  it’s |  biggest customer.
why correct: The customer belongs to the company, so the possessive “its” (no apostrophe) is needed.
tip: Possessive pronouns (its, yours, theirs) never use apostrophes.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which word is an adjective? “The tiny kitten slept on the rug.”
options / answer: A) slept | B) tiny | C) kitten | D) on
why correct: “Tiny” describes the kitten (what kind).
tip: Adjectives tell what kind, how many or how much.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence capitalizes the proper adjective correctly?
options / answer: A) We tasted delicious Lebanese Bread. | B) We tasted delicious lebanese bread. | C) We tasted delicious Lebanese bread. | D) We tasted Delicious Lebanese bread.
why correct: “Lebanese” comes from the proper noun Lebanon, so it is capitalized.
tip: Proper adjectives come from proper nouns.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Choose the article: “She ate ____ orange after lunch.”
options / answer: A) a | B) an | C) the | D) this
why correct: “Orange” begins with a vowel sound, so use “an.”
tip: a + consonant sound; an + vowel sound.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Choose the demonstrative adjective: “____ books right here on my desk are new.”
options / answer: A) That | B) Those | C) These | D) This
why correct: Plural and near → “these.”
tip: this/these = near; that/those = far.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which phrase lists the adjectives in the correct order?
options / answer: A) old two beautiful chairs | B) beautiful two old chairs | C) two old beautiful chairs | D) two beautiful old chairs
why correct: The order is number, opinion, size, age, color: two (number) beautiful (opinion) old (age).
tip: Number → opinion → size → age → color.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence uses commas with adjectives correctly?
options / answer: A) Jorge played a quiet, gentle song on the oud. | B) Jorge played a quiet gentle, song on the oud. | C) Jorge played a, quiet gentle song on the oud. | D) Jorge played three, quiet songs on the oud.
why correct: Two adjectives that equally describe the noun are separated by a comma.
tip: Test: if you can put “and” between the adjectives, use a comma.

stem: Choose the past tense: “Yesterday, Amal ____ the ball.”
options / answer: A) catches | B) catched | C) catching | D) caught
why correct: catch → caught.
tip: Irregular verbs do not add -ed in the past tense.

stem: Choose the past tense: “Last week, we ____ a new route to school.”
options / answer: A) chose | B) choosed | C) choose | D) chosen
why correct: choose → chose (past) → have chosen (past participle).
tip: Learn the three forms of irregular verbs.

stem: Match each verb with its past tense.
options / answer: bring = brought | begin = began | keep = kept | drink = drank
why correct: Each of these verbs forms its past tense irregularly.
tip: Say “Yesterday I…” to test the past tense.

stem: Choose the correct form: “By noon, the guests had ____ all the dates.”
options / answer: A) eated | B) eaten | C) eat | D) ate
why correct: had + past participle: had eaten.
tip: Past tense stands alone (ate); the past participle follows have/has/had (eaten).

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The leaves |  falled |  from the trees |  in the strong wind.
why correct: “Fall” is irregular: the past tense is “fell.”
tip: If a past tense sounds strange with -ed, check whether the verb is irregular.

stem: Which sentence uses irregular verbs correctly?
options / answer: A) She knew the answer because she had red the chapter twice. | B) She knew the answer because she had read the chapter twice. | C) She knowed the answer because she had readed the chapter twice. | D) She known the answer because she had read the chapter twice.
why correct: knew (past of know) and had read (past participle of read) are both correct.
tip: Some irregular verbs, like read, keep the same spelling but change pronunciation.

stem: Which sentence uses negatives correctly?
options / answer: A) I didn’t do nothing wrong. | B) I not did nothing wrong. | C) I didn’t do anything wrong. | D) I didn’t never do anything wrong.
why correct: Use only one negative per clause: “didn’t” + the positive word “anything.”
tip: Do not use two negatives in the same clause.

stem: Choose the correct word: “Nobody ____ where the key is.”
options / answer: A) doesn’t know | B) don’t know | C) knows | D) never knows
why correct: “Nobody knows” has one negative, which is correct.
tip: Negative words include no, not, nobody, nothing, never, no one and nowhere.

stem: “We don’t want to go nowhere today” is correct.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: It is a double negative. Correct: “We don’t want to go anywhere today.”
tip: Replace one negative with its positive form.

stem: Choose the correct word: “There isn’t ____ milk left in the fridge.”
options / answer: A) no | B) nothing | C) none | D) any
why correct: “Isn’t” is already negative, so use the positive word “any.”
tip: After a negative verb, use any, anything, anyone, ever or anywhere.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The new student |  hasn’t |  met nobody |  in our class yet.
why correct: “Hasn’t” is negative, so the second word must be positive: “anybody.”
tip: Check each clause for more than one negative word.

stem: Which pair of revisions BOTH correct “She never says nothing in class”?
options / answer: A) “She always says nothing” or “She never says nothing” | B) “She doesn’t never say anything” or “She never says nothing” | C) “She never doesn’t say anything in class” or “She says nothing never” | D) “She never says anything in class” or “She says nothing in class”
why correct: Remove one negative (says nothing) or change one to a positive (never says anything).
tip: A double negative can be fixed two ways: remove one negative, or make it positive.

stem: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options / answer: A) We visited Riyadh in March. | B) We visited riyadh in March. | C) We visited Riyadh in march. | D) we visited Riyadh in March.
why correct: Cities, months and the first word of a sentence are capitalized.
tip: Capitalize names of places, days, months and holidays.

stem: Which group of words is capitalized correctly?
options / answer: A) the Red Sea, the Battle of Badr, saudi national day | B) the Red Sea, the Battle of Badr, Saudi National Day | C) the red sea, the Battle of Badr, Saudi National Day | D) the Red Sea, the battle of badr, Saudi National Day
why correct: Geographical names, historical events and holidays are all proper nouns.
tip: Capitalize each important word in a multi-word proper noun.

stem: Which abbreviation is written correctly?
options / answer: A) Dr A K Hamdi | B) dr. A.K. Hamdi | C) Dr. A.K. Hamdi | D) Dr. a.k. Hamdi
why correct: Titles and initials are capitalized and end with a period.
tip: Initial = first letter of a name, capitalized with a period.

stem: Acronyms such as NASA and the UN are usually written in all capital letters without periods.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: This matches the rule for acronyms in your grammar book.
tip: Acronyms are formed from the first letters of words in a name.

stem: Which closing for a letter is capitalized correctly?
options / answer: A) Best Wishes, | B) BEST WISHES, | C) best wishes, | D) Best wishes,
why correct: In a closing, capitalize only the first word.
tip: Greeting: capitalize the first word and names. Closing: first word only.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: Last thurs., |  Mrs. Jackson |  read an article |  about the American Heart Association.
why correct: Abbreviations of days are capitalized: Thurs.
tip: Abbreviations of proper nouns keep their capital letters.

stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options / answer: A) “I finished my project,” said Nouf. | B) “I finished my project” said Nouf. | C) “I finished my project”, said Nouf. | D) I finished my project, said Nouf.
why correct: Quotation marks go around the speaker’s words, with the comma inside.
tip: Commas and periods go inside closing quotation marks.

stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options / answer: A) Coach said “Practice starts at four.” | B) Coach said, “Practice starts at four.” | C) Coach said, “practice starts at four.” | D) Coach said, “Practice starts at four”.
why correct: A comma separates the speaker tag from the quotation; the period goes inside.
tip: Speaker tag + comma + “Quotation.”

stem: There should be a space between an opening quotation mark and the first word of the quotation.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: There is no space after an opening quotation mark or before a closing one.
tip: Quotation marks sit right next to the words they enclose.

stem: Where do the commas belong? “If we hurry” said Omar “we can catch the bus.”
options / answer: A) Only after “Omar” | B) No commas are needed | C) After “hurry” (inside the quotation mark) and after “Omar” | D) After “we” and after “said”
why correct: Correct: “If we hurry,” said Omar, “we can catch the bus.”
tip: When a speaker tag interrupts a sentence, use commas on both sides of it.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: “Mom, I had so much fun at the party” |  Charlie said | .
correct: segment 1 → “Mom, I had so much fun at the party,”
why correct: The comma belongs inside the closing quotation mark.
tip: Commas and periods always go inside closing quotation marks.

stem: Put the pieces in order to make a correctly punctuated sentence.
options / answer: “When the bell rings,” → said the teacher, → “please line up quietly.”
why correct: The quotation is interrupted by the speaker tag, with commas on both sides.
tip: An interrupted quotation: “Part one,” speaker tag, “part two.”

stem: What makes this a pun? “The baker quit because he couldn’t make enough dough.”
options / answer: A) It repeats the same sound at the start. | B) It compares a baker to money using “like.” | C) It rhymes “baker” and “dough.” | D) “Dough” means both bread mixture and, informally, money.
why correct: A pun plays on a word with two meanings; “dough” can mean bread mixture or money.
tip: A pun is a joke that uses a word’s double meaning.

stem: Which sentence is a pun?
options / answer: A) I used to be a banker, but I lost interest. | B) Banks open at nine o’clock. | C) I worked at the bank for ten years. | D) My bank is next to the bakery.
why correct: “Interest” means both money a bank pays and curiosity.
tip: Look for one word that makes sense in two ways.

stem: “The math book looked sad because it had too many problems” is a pun.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: “Problems” means both math exercises and troubles.
tip: Ask whether one word works with two different meanings.

stem: Which word creates the pun? “Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana.”
options / answer: A) arrow | B) flies | C) time | D) banana
why correct: “Flies” is a verb (moves quickly) in the first part and a noun (insects) in the second.
tip: Puns can switch a word between two parts of speech.

stem: Match each pun with the word that has the double meaning.
options / answer: The tailor won because he was always on pins and needles. = pins and needles | The bicycle couldn’t stand up because it was two-tired. = two-tired | The scarecrow got an award for being outstanding in his field. = outstanding in his field
why correct: Each pun depends on a word or phrase that sounds like or means two things.
tip: Find the phrase that makes the reader smile.

stem: Why might an author use a pun in a historical story?
options / answer: A) To give exact dates and facts | B) To replace dialogue | C) To show a character’s cleverness or add humor | D) To make the story sound more serious
why correct: Puns reveal a playful or witty character and give readers a moment of humor.
tip: Think about the effect of wordplay on the reader.

stem: You want to know whether “record” in your sentence is a noun or a verb. Which part of the dictionary entry should you check?
options / answer: A) The number of syllables | B) The guide words at the top of the page | C) The first letter of the entry word | D) The part-of-speech label, such as (n.) or (v.)
why correct: Dictionary entries label each meaning with its part of speech, such as noun or verb.
tip: Look for small labels like n., v., adj. after the entry word.

stem: A digital thesaurus lists “glance, peek, scan, gaze” for “look.” Which word means to look for a long time?
options / answer: A) gaze | B) peek | C) glance | D) scan
why correct: To gaze is to look steadily for a long time, often with wonder.
tip: Synonyms have shades of meaning; check the dictionary to choose precisely.

stem: The dictionary shows “con·duct (noun) KON-dukt; (verb) kuhn-DUKT.” How should you say “conduct” in “The students will conduct an experiment”?
options / answer: A) KON-dukt, because it is a noun | B) kuhn-DUKT, because it is a verb | C) Either way, because the meaning is the same | D) KON-DUKT, stressing both syllables
why correct: “Will conduct” is a verb, so the stress is on the second syllable.
tip: Some words change stress depending on their part of speech.

stem: A glossary is found at the back of a book and defines words used in that book.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Unlike a dictionary, a glossary only covers words from that book.
tip: Glossary = mini-dictionary for one book.

stem: Which source should you use to check whether “principal” or “principle” fits your sentence?
options / answer: A) An almanac | B) A table of contents | C) A dictionary, to compare the meanings | D) An atlas
why correct: A dictionary gives each word’s meaning so you can choose correctly.
tip: Use a dictionary for meaning and spelling; a thesaurus for synonyms.

stem: Put these words in dictionary order.
options / answer: harbinger → harbor → hardship → harmony → harvest
why correct: Compare letter by letter: harb-i, harb-o, hard, harm, harv.
tip: When words begin the same way, keep comparing until a letter differs.

stem: What does the suffix -less mean in “spotless”?
options / answer: A) full of | B) one who | C) again | D) without
why correct: Spotless means without spots, completely clean.
tip: -less = without; -ful = full of.

stem: What does “washable” mean?
options / answer: A) able to be washed | B) already washed | C) one who washes things | D) full of water
why correct: The suffix -able means able to be: washable = able to be washed.
tip: Add the meaning of the suffix to the base word.

stem: Choose the word that means “the state of being kind”: “Her ____ made everyone feel welcome.”
options / answer: A) kindness | B) kindly | C) kinder | D) unkind
why correct: The suffix -ness turns an adjective into a noun meaning “the state of being.”
tip: -ness = state or quality of.

stem: Match each suffix with its meaning.
options / answer: -ful = full of | -less = without | -ment = the act or result of | -er = one who
why correct: Knowing suffix meanings helps you figure out new words.
tip: Think of a word you know with each suffix.

stem: Which word means “in a careful way”?
options / answer: A) careless | B) carefully | C) careful | D) caring
why correct: care + -ful (full of) + -ly (in a … way) = in a careful way.
tip: Some words have two suffixes; build the meaning step by step.

stem: In “The government announced a new agreement,” how do the suffixes help you understand “government” and “agreement”?
options / answer: A) -ment turns the nouns into verbs. | B) -ment means “without.” | C) -ment turns the verbs “govern” and “agree” into nouns. | D) -ment makes the words plural.
why correct: Govern → government; agree → agreement. Both become nouns naming a thing or result.
tip: Suffixes can change a word’s part of speech.

stem: Choose the verb: “The scientist ____ through the microscope.”
options / answer: A) look | B) looks | C) looking | D) are looking
why correct: “Scientist” is singular, so the verb adds -s: looks.
tip: Singular subject → verb + s. Plural subject → no -s.

stem: Choose the verb: “Audrey and her sister ____ catch in the field.”
options / answer: A) has played | B) plays | C) play | D) is playing
why correct: Two people joined by “and” make a plural subject, so the verb has no -s.
tip: Subject + and + subject = plural.

stem: Choose the verb: “The box of old toys ____ dust in the attic.”
options / answer: A) are collecting | B) have collected | C) collect | D) collects
why correct: The prepositional phrase “of old toys” does not change the subject; “box” is singular.
tip: Cross out prepositional phrases to find the real subject.

stem: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?
options / answer: A) A flock of birds fly over the river every evening. | B) A flocks of birds flies over the river every evening. | C) A flock of birds flying over the river every evening. | D) A flock of birds flies over the river every evening.
why correct: “Flock” is a collective noun referring to the group as a whole, so it takes a singular verb.
tip: Collective nouns (flock, team, class) usually take singular verbs.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: My sisters practice basketball, |  and my little brother |  watch |  from the bench.
why correct: In a compound sentence, each subject agrees with its own verb: “brother” is singular, so “watches.”
tip: Check the verb in each clause of a compound sentence separately.

stem: Which sentence is correct?
options / answer: A) Each of the students has a locker. | B) Each of the students having a locker. | C) Each of the student have a locker. | D) Each of the students have a locker.
why correct: The subject is “Each,” which is singular, so the verb is “has.”
tip: Words like each, every and either are singular subjects.

stem: What is the role of the NARRATOR in “The Interview”?
options / answer: A) To interview Mr. Aziz | B) To introduce the setting and situation before the action begins | C) To play a character in the interview | D) To give stage directions to actors
why correct: The narrator explains when and where the play takes place and why Sara is there.
tip: A narrator in a play speaks to the audience to provide background.

stem: What is an aside, as used by Sara in Scene 1?
options / answer: A) A change of scene | B) A long speech to another character | C) A comment spoken to the audience that other characters do not hear | D) A stage direction about where to stand
why correct: Sara’s aside reveals her frustration to the audience without Mr. Aziz hearing it.
tip: Asides let the audience know a character’s private thoughts.

stem: In “The Interview,” Scene 2 takes place two hours after Scene 1.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The stage directions for Scene 2 say “Two hours later.”
tip: Scene headings and stage directions show changes in time and place.

stem: How does the stage direction [stopping, then smiling for the first time] contribute to the plot?
options / answer: A) It explains why the gym flooded. | B) It shows that Mr. Aziz is finished working for the day. | C) It introduces a new character. | D) It marks the turning point when Mr. Aziz begins to open up.
why correct: After this moment his short answers change into a long story, which shifts the interview.
tip: Stage directions can mark important changes in a character or in the plot.

stem: Which line from “Desert Night” appeals mainly to the sense of taste?

stem: What does the simile “like a coin into a pocket” suggest about the sunset?
options / answer: A) The sun is made of metal. | B) Someone has stolen the sun. | C) The sunset is very slow. | D) The sun disappears quickly and neatly below the dunes.
why correct: A coin slips out of sight smoothly and fast, like the sun sinking.
tip: A simile compares two things using like or as.

stem: “The coffee pot hisses on the coals” appeals to the sense of hearing.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: “Hisses” is a sound word.
tip: Sound words create auditory imagery.

stem: What does the metaphor “the sky unrolls its black carpet, scattered with salt” describe?
options / answer: A) The night sky spreading out, full of white stars | B) A sandstorm covering the sky | C) Salt being spilled on a rug | D) Black clouds before rain
why correct: The black carpet is the dark sky, and the scattered salt is the stars.
tip: A metaphor describes one thing as if it were another.

stem: Match each image from “Desert Night” with the sense it appeals to most.
options / answer: the sand gives back the day’s heat = Touch | a camel groans, low as a cello string = Hearing | bitter and gold with cardamom = Taste | the sky unrolls its black carpet = Sight
why correct: The poet uses every sense to place the reader in the desert.
tip: Identify the sense each detail relies on.

stem: How does the imagery in the last two lines shift the poem’s focus?
options / answer: A) From night to morning | B) From the wide desert landscape to the speaker’s close, personal experience | C) From calm to frightening | D) From the speaker to the camel
why correct: “I hold the small cup with both hands” brings the reader close to the speaker’s senses.
tip: Notice when a poem moves from wide images to close-up ones.

stem: What is the subject of the command “Close the window, please”?
options / answer: A) There is no subject. | B) window | C) you (understood) | D) please
why correct: In an imperative sentence, the subject “you” is understood.
tip: Commands have an understood subject.

stem: What is the simple subject? “Neither of the answers on the board was correct.”
options / answer: A) answers | B) correct | C) board | D) Neither
why correct: Remove “of the answers on the board”; the subject is “Neither.”
tip: The subject is never inside a prepositional phrase.

stem: Find the subject: “Here are the results of the survey.”
options / answer: A) results | B) survey | C) Here | D) are
why correct: Rearranged: “The results of the survey are here.” The subject is “results.”
tip: In sentences beginning with here or there, the subject follows the verb.

stem: In “The team and its coach celebrated and posed for photos,” the sentence has a compound subject and a compound predicate.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: Subjects: team, coach. Predicates: celebrated, posed.
tip: Find all subjects, then all verbs.

stem: What is the complete predicate? “During the storm, the old fishing boat drifted slowly toward the rocks.”
options / answer: A) the old fishing boat | B) drifted slowly toward the rocks | C) During the storm, the old fishing boat | D) toward the rocks
why correct: The complete predicate is the verb and everything that tells about it.
tip: Introductory phrases are not part of the subject.

stem: Write the simple predicate (main verb phrase): “By next June, the new library will have opened its doors.” ____
options / answer: (typed)
why correct: The simple predicate includes all helping verbs: will have opened.
tip: Include every helping verb in the simple predicate.

stem: Which compound sentence is punctuated correctly?
options / answer: A) The museum closed early but, the café stayed open. | B) The museum closed early, the café stayed open. | C) The museum closed early, but the café stayed open. | D) The museum, closed early but the café stayed open.
why correct: Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses.
tip: FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.

stem: Which sentence correctly uses a semicolon?
options / answer: A) The rain stopped the; players returned. | B) The rain; stopped the players returned. | C) The rain stopped; and the players returned. | D) The rain stopped; the players returned to the field.
why correct: A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction.
tip: Each side of a semicolon should be a complete sentence.

stem: Choose the conjunction: “He was exhausted, ____ he finished the race.”
options / answer: A) yet | B) or | C) so | D) for
why correct: “Yet” shows a surprising contrast.
tip: yet/but = contrast; so = result; for = reason; or = choice.

stem: Choose the conjunction: “Neither the coach was ready, ____ were the players.”
options / answer: A) and | B) nor | C) or | D) but
why correct: “Neither … nor” is a correlative pair.
tip: Pairs: either/or, neither/nor, both/and, not only/but also.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The library was quiet | , students |  read silently |  at every table.
why correct: Two independent clauses joined only by a comma create a comma splice; use a semicolon (or add a conjunction).
tip: A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences.

stem: Which revision best combines the ideas to show cause and effect? “The bridge was closed. Traffic moved slowly all morning.”
options / answer: A) The bridge was closed, so traffic moved slowly all morning. | B) The bridge was closed, but traffic moved slowly all morning. | C) The bridge was closed, traffic moved slowly all morning. | D) The bridge was closed, or traffic moved slowly all morning.
why correct: “So” shows that the closed bridge caused the slow traffic.
tip: Choose the conjunction that matches the logical relationship.

stem: Which word is an adverb? “The choir sang beautifully at the ceremony.”
options / answer: A) choir | B) beautifully | C) ceremony | D) sang
why correct: “Beautifully” tells how the choir sang.
tip: Adverbs tell how, when, where or to what extent.

stem: What question does the adverb answer? “We will leave tomorrow.”
options / answer: A) To what extent? | B) Where? | C) When? | D) How?
why correct: “Tomorrow” tells when we will leave.
tip: Adverbs of time: today, soon, later, tomorrow.

stem: Choose the relative adverb: “I still remember the day ____ we moved to a new city.”
options / answer: A) where | B) why | C) when | D) which
why correct: “When” introduces a clause that tells about a time: the day.
tip: Relative adverbs: where (place), when (time), why (reason).

stem: Choose the correct form: “Of all the runners, Nasser finished ____.”
options / answer: A) more quickly | B) quickliest | C) most quick | D) most quickly

tip: -ly adverbs: more/most + adverb.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: She did |  good |  on the test |  this morning.

tip: Use well (adverb) to describe actions; good (adjective) to describe nouns.

stem: Which word does the adverb “extremely” modify? “The extremely tired hikers rested by the stream.”
options / answer: A) stream | B) hikers | C) rested | D) tired
why correct: “Extremely” modifies the adjective “tired,” telling to what extent.
tip: Adverbs can modify verbs, adjectives or other adverbs.

stem: Choose the correct word: “____ turn is it to present?”
options / answer: A) Whose | B) Who | C) Who’s | D) Whos
why correct: “Whose” shows ownership: whose turn.
tip: Who’s = who is/who has; whose = belonging to whom.

stem: Choose the correct word: “The students said ____ ready to present their project.”

tip: Expand the contraction to check if it fits.

stem: Which sentence uses its and it’s correctly?

stem: Match each word with its meaning.
options / answer: your = belonging to you | you’re = you are | who’s = who is | whose = belonging to whom
why correct: Contractions contain apostrophes; possessive pronouns do not.
tip: Replace the word with its expanded form to test it.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

tip: Check each your/you’re in the sentence separately.

stem: Which sentence is completely correct?

tip: Test every homophone in a long sentence one at a time.

stem: What does the prefix mis- mean in “misunderstand”?

stem: Using the prefix inter- (between), what does “international” mean?

tip: Combine the prefix meaning with the base word.

stem: In “The scientist’s findings were later proven to be a misinterpretation,” what does the prefix help you understand?

tip: Prefixes change meaning even in long academic words.

tip: Relative adverbs: where (place), when (time), why (reason).

tip: Use an adverb to describe a verb.

tip: Two things: -er. Three or more: -est.

tip: “Of the three” signals a superlative.

tip: Long words: more/most. Short words: -er/-est.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

tip: Never double up comparing words.

stem: Which sentence uses comparing words correctly?

stem: “Ran to the gate” is a complete sentence.

tip: Fix run-ons with a period, or a comma and a conjunction.

stem: Which revision fixes the fragment? “When the bell rang. We lined up.”

tip: A clause starting with “When” needs a main clause.

stem: Choose the past tense: “Yesterday I ____ to the market.”
options / answer: A) goed | B) went | C) goes | D) going

tip: Irregular verbs change their spelling in the past.

stem: Choose the past tense: “Last night Mama ____ a story.”
options / answer: A) tolled | B) telled | C) told | D) tells

stem: Match each verb with its past tense.

tip: Many irregular verbs change a vowel.

stem: Choose the correct form: “Have you ever ____ a camel?”
options / answer: A) rode | B) ride | C) rided | D) ridden

tip: ride → rode → (have) ridden.

stem: Which sentence uses irregular verbs correctly?
options / answer: A) The bell rang, and the students began to write. | B) The bell rang, and the students begun to write. | C) The bell ringed, and the students began to write. | D) The bell rung, and the students began to write.

tip: Past tense stands alone; past participles need has/have/had.

stem: Which word is a negative?

tip: Negatives: no, not, never, nobody, nothing, nowhere.

stem: Choose the correct word: “I don’t have ____ homework tonight.”
options / answer: A) any | B) none | C) nothing | D) no

tip: One negative per sentence.

stem: “Nobody never cleans the board” is correct.
options / answer: True | False

tip: Change one negative to a positive word.

stem: Choose the correct word: “There wasn’t ____ in the box.”
options / answer: A) none | B) anything | C) nothing | D) nobody

tip: After n’t, use any-words.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: We couldn’t find |  our cat |  nowhere |  in the house.
why correct: “Couldn’t” is already negative, so “nowhere” must become “anywhere.”
tip: Look for n’t plus another negative.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: Which TWO words are nouns? “The farmer fed the hungry goats.”

why correct: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea.
tip: Test: can you put “the” before it?

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: Which word is an abstract noun (an idea or feeling)?
options / answer: A) teacher | B) helmet | C) garden | D) courage
why correct: Courage is a quality you cannot see or touch.
tip: Abstract nouns name ideas and feelings.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: Which word is a collective noun?
options / answer: A) flock | B) feather | C) bird | D) nest
why correct: A collective noun names a group: a flock of birds.
tip: Collective nouns: team, class, family, flock, herd.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: In “Her kindness surprised the whole class,” which words are nouns?
options / answer: A) Her, kindness | B) kindness, class | C) kindness, surprised | D) whole, class
why correct: “Kindness” is an abstract noun; “class” is a collective noun.
tip: Nouns can be people, places, things or ideas.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: Choose the plural: “I have two ____.”
options / answer: A) pencil’s | B) pencil | C) pencils | D) pencilss
why correct: Most nouns add -s to make plurals.
tip: Add -s to most nouns.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: Choose the plural: “The ____ played in the yard.”
options / answer: A) puppy’s | B) puppyes | C) puppys | D) puppies
why correct: puppy → puppies.
tip: Consonant + y → -ies.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: Which sentence uses plural nouns correctly?
options / answer: A) The women gave the childrens some knives and forks. | B) The women gave the children some knifes and forks. | C) The women gave the children some knives and forks. | D) The womans gave the childs some knifes and forks.
why correct: women, children, knives are irregular plurals.
tip: Learn irregular plurals by heart.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: Match each singular noun with its plural.
options / answer: mouse = mice | tooth = teeth | wolf = wolves | sheep = sheep
why correct: These plurals do not just add -s.
tip: Some plurals change vowels or stay the same.

stem: Which word is a preposition? “The ball rolled under the car.”
options / answer: A) rolled | B) ball | C) car | D) under
why correct: “Under” shows where the ball rolled.
tip: Prepositions show position or direction.

stem: Choose the preposition: “Put the books ____ the shelf.”
options / answer: A) on | B) blue | C) slowly | D) books
why correct: “On” shows where to put the books.
tip: Common prepositions: on, in, under, over, between, behind.

stem: What is the object of the preposition? “We walked along the narrow path.”
options / answer: A) path | B) narrow | C) walked | D) along
why correct: The object is the noun after the preposition: path.
tip: Preposition + (describing words) + noun = phrase.

stem: Which TWO are prepositional phrases? “After school, the cat slept beside the window.”
options / answer: A) slept beside | B) After school | C) beside the window | D) the cat slept
why correct: Each phrase starts with a preposition and ends with a noun.
tip: Find the preposition, then its noun.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The keys |  were hidden |  between of |  the cushions.
why correct: “Between” is the preposition; “of” is not needed.
tip: Use one preposition before the object.

stem: Choose the correct word: “Is this ____ backpack?”
options / answer: A) yore | B) your | C) youre | D) you’re
why correct: “Your” shows ownership.
tip: your = belongs to you; you’re = you are.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: They put |  there coats |  on the hooks |  by the door.
why correct: The coats belong to them, so use “their.”
tip: their = belonging to them.

stem: Which sentence is correct?
options / answer: A) They’re bringing there kites over their. | B) They’re bringing their kites over there. | C) There bringing their kites over they’re. | D) Their bringing there kites over they’re.
why correct: They’re = they are; their = belonging to them; there = a place.
tip: Test each word separately.

stem: Which pronoun can replace “Sara” in “Sara likes art”?
options / answer: A) It | B) They | C) She | D) He
why correct: Sara is one girl, so “she.”
tip: Pronouns take the place of nouns.

stem: Choose the pronoun: “Mom gave the gift to ____.”
options / answer: A) I | B) mine | C) me | D) myself
why correct: After “to,” use the object pronoun “me.”
tip: I is a subject; me is an object.

stem: Choose the relative pronoun: “The book ____ I borrowed was exciting.”
options / answer: A) who | B) whose | C) where | D) that
why correct: “That” refers to things like the book.
tip: who = people; which/that = things.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: Ali and me |  finished |  the puzzle |  together.
why correct: As part of the subject, use “I.” Test: “I finished,” not “me finished.”
tip: Remove the other person to test.

stem: Which sentence is a command?
options / answer: A) Is the door closed? | B) What a heavy door! | C) The door is closed. | D) Please close the door.
why correct: A command tells someone to do something.
tip: Commands often begin with a verb.

stem: Choose the end mark: “What a beautiful sunset____”
why correct: Exclamations show strong feeling.
tip: ! = strong feeling.

stem: Match each sentence with its type.
options / answer: The museum opens at nine. = Statement | When does the museum open? = Question | Buy the tickets now. = Command | What an amazing museum! = Exclamation
why correct: Each type has a purpose and an end mark.
tip: Look at the end mark and the purpose.

stem: Which sentence is a statement that ends correctly?
options / answer: A) The train leaves at noon. | B) Does the train leave at noon. | C) the train leaves at noon. | D) The train leaves at noon?
why correct: A statement tells something and ends with a period.
tip: Capital letter at the start, period at the end.

stem: Change the statement into a question: “Laila can speak three languages.”
options / answer: A) Can Laila speaks three languages? | B) Can Laila speak three languages? | C) Laila can speak, three languages? | D) Laila can speak three languages?
why correct: Move the helping verb “can” to the front to form a question.
tip: Questions often start with a helping verb.

stem: Choose the verb: “The dog ____ at the mail carrier.”
options / answer: A) barking | B) barks | C) bark | D) are barking
why correct: One dog → barks.
tip: Singular subject → verb with -s.

stem: Choose the verb: “My brothers ____ football every Friday.”
options / answer: A) is playing | B) has played | C) play | D) plays
why correct: Plural subject → no -s: play.
tip: Plural subject → verb without -s.

stem: Choose the verb: “The plates on the shelf ____ clean.”
options / answer: A) has been | B) was | C) is | D) are
why correct: “On the shelf” does not change the subject; “plates” is plural, so “are.”
tip: Cover the prepositional phrase to find the real subject.

stem: Which sentence has correct agreement?
options / answer: A) Either my aunt or my uncle drive us to school. | B) Either my aunt or my uncle have driven us. | C) Either my aunt or my uncle drives us to school. | D) Either my aunt or my uncle are driving us to school.
why correct: With “either … or,” the verb agrees with the nearer subject: uncle drives.
tip: or/nor: match the closest subject.

stem: Choose the FUTURE tense: “Tomorrow we ____ the zoo.”
options / answer: A) will visit | B) visit | C) visiting | D) visited
why correct: “Will” + verb shows the future.
tip: Future = will + verb.

stem: Which sentence is in the PAST tense?
options / answer: A) We paint the fence today. | B) We are painting the fence now. | C) We will paint the fence tomorrow. | D) We painted the fence yesterday.
why correct: “Painted” and “yesterday” show the past.
tip: Time words help show tense.

stem: Choose the verb (present progressive): “Look! The bus ____ right now.”
options / answer: A) was leaving | B) is leaving | C) will leave | D) left
why correct: “Right now” shows an action happening now: is leaving.
tip: Present progressive = am/is/are + -ing.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: Yesterday |  we walk |  to the park |  and fed the ducks.
why correct: “Yesterday” and “fed” show the past, so “walk” must be “walked.”
tip: Keep verb tenses consistent.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Which word is an action verb? “The baby giggled at the clown.”
options / answer: A) giggled | B) at | C) baby | D) clown
why correct: “Giggled” shows an action.
tip: Action verbs show what someone does.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Which word is a linking verb? “The soup is hot.”
options / answer: A) soup | B) is | C) hot | D) The
why correct: “Is” links the soup to the word that describes it.
tip: Linking verbs: am, is, are, was, were, seem, become.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Choose the helping verb: “The students ____ finished their projects.”
options / answer: A) is | B) having | C) have | D) has
why correct: “Have finished” is a verb phrase with a helping verb.
tip: Helping verbs: have, has, had, is, are, will, can.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Which modal verb shows possibility? “It ____ rain this afternoon.”
options / answer: A) will | B) shall | C) might | D) must
why correct: “Might” shows something possible but not certain.
tip: might/may = possible; must = required.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Which TWO words are verbs? “Huda seemed tired, so she rested.”
options / answer: A) seemed | B) so | C) tired | D) rested
why correct: “Seemed” is a linking verb; “rested” is an action verb.
tip: Find every word that shows action or links.

stem: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options / answer: A) on Friday, we visited the Red Sea Museum. | B) On friday, we visited the Red Sea Museum. | C) On Friday, we visited the red sea museum. | D) On Friday, we visited the Red Sea Museum.
why correct: Capitalize days, names of places and the first word.
tip: Proper nouns get capitals.

stem: Which title is capitalized correctly?
options / answer: A) The Boy Who Planted Trees | B) The Boy who Planted trees | C) the Boy Who Planted Trees | D) The boy who planted trees
why correct: Capitalize the first word and the important words in a title.
tip: Short words like “a” and “of” stay lowercase unless first.

stem: Which sentence capitalizes a family title correctly?
options / answer: A) Yesterday my Grandma told us a story. | B) Yesterday Grandma told us a story. | C) yesterday Grandma told us a story. | D) Yesterday grandma told us a story.
why correct: Family titles used as names are capitalized; after “my” they are not.
tip: Test: can you replace it with a name?

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: My cousin |  moved to |  dammam |  in August.
why correct: City names are proper nouns and need capital letters.
tip: Capitalize the names of cities and countries.

stem: Which sentence uses commas in a list correctly?
options / answer: A) We bought dates, figs, and, grapes. | B) We bought, dates, figs, and grapes. | C) We bought dates, figs, and grapes. | D) We bought dates figs and grapes.
why correct: Commas separate three or more items in a series.
tip: Use commas between items in a list.

stem: Which sentence uses a comma after an introductory word correctly?
options / answer: A) Yes I would like some tea | B) Yes I, would like some tea. | C) Yes I would like, some tea. | D) Yes, I would like some tea.
why correct: Use a comma after an introductory word such as yes, no or well.
tip: Pause words at the start get a comma.

stem: Which sentence uses a comma in direct address correctly?
options / answer: A) Fatima, please hand me the ruler. | B) Fatima please, hand me the ruler. | C) Fatima, please hand, me the ruler. | D) Fatima please hand me the ruler.
why correct: Use a comma to set off the name of the person being spoken to.
tip: Name + comma when you speak to someone.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: On March 3 |  2026 |  the new library |  opened its doors.
why correct: A comma goes between the day and the year in a date.
tip: Dates: month day, year.

stem: Which sentence uses ALL commas correctly?
options / answer: A) Well Rania, we need flour, eggs, and milk before Tuesday March 12. | B) Well, Rania, we need flour, eggs, and milk before Tuesday, March 12. | C) Well, Rania, we need, flour, eggs, and milk before Tuesday, March 12. | D) Well, Rania we need flour eggs, and milk before Tuesday, March 12.
why correct: Commas follow the introductory word, set off the name, separate list items and separate the day from the date.
tip: Check each comma rule one at a time.

stem: Which words should be inside quotation marks? Majed said I love reading.
options / answer: A) Majed said I love reading | B) Majed said | C) I love reading | D) said I
why correct: Quotation marks go around the exact words someone says.
tip: Put only the spoken words inside.

stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options / answer: A) “Let’s go to the beach” said Hessa. | B) Let’s go to the beach, said Hessa. | C) “Let’s go to the beach”, said Hessa. | D) “Let’s go to the beach,” said Hessa.
why correct: The comma goes inside the closing quotation marks.
tip: Comma, then closing quotation mark.

stem: Which question is punctuated correctly?
options / answer: A) “Where is my notebook?” asked Saad. | B) Where is my notebook? asked Saad. | C) “Where is my notebook,” asked Saad. | D) “Where is my notebook”? asked Saad.
why correct: A question mark that belongs to the quotation goes inside the quotation marks.
tip: The end mark stays with the spoken words.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: Mr. Saleh said,  | “please line up quietly.”
why correct: The first word of a quotation that is a complete sentence is capitalized.
tip: Start quotations with a capital letter.

stem: Put the pieces in order to make a correctly punctuated sentence.
options / answer: “After lunch,” → said Coach, → “we will practice passing.”
why correct: The speaker tag interrupts the quotation and is set off by commas.
tip: Interrupted quotation: “part one,” tag, “part two.”

stem: Which sentence from “Our School Needs a Garden” states the author’s claim?
options / answer: A) “The empty lot is wasted space right now.” | B) “Our school should turn the empty lot behind the library into a vegetable garden.” | C) “Learning by doing helps facts stick.” | D) “Each class could care for its own bed.”
why correct: The first sentence tells exactly what the author wants the school to do.
tip: The claim is often in the first sentence.

stem: Which piece of evidence would make the garden argument STRONGER?
options / answer: A) A sentence saying gardens are pretty | B) A list of all the classes in the school | C) A survey showing students ate more vegetables after a nearby school started a garden | D) A picture of the author’s favorite flower
why correct: Real data that matches one of the author’s reasons strengthens the claim.
tip: Facts and data are stronger than opinions.

stem: How does the author of “Our School Needs a Garden” feel about the empty lot?
options / answer: A) It is too small for anything. | B) It should stay empty. | C) It is the best part of the school. | D) It is being wasted.
why correct: The author calls it “wasted space right now.”
tip: Look for words that show feelings.

stem: Which word in “The Dripping Taps” shows how the author first viewed the problem?
options / answer: A) worrying | B) full | C) lower | D) bright
why correct: The students “noticed something worrying,” which shows concern.
tip: Authors reveal their view through word choice.

stem: The author of “Nature’s Engineers” thinks beavers only cause problems.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The author admits dams can flood roads but says many scientists think benefits are greater.
tip: Check whether the author presents more than one side.

stem: How does the author of “Nature’s Engineers” show a balanced point of view?
options / answer: A) By describing only how beavers build lodges | B) By mentioning that dams can flood roads, then explaining why scientists still value beavers | C) By telling a story about one beaver | D) By saying beavers are dangerous to people
why correct: The last paragraph admits problems and weighs them against benefits.
tip: Balanced writing presents more than one side.

stem: How does the author of “The Dripping Taps” show the students’ success instead of just giving an opinion?
options / answer: A) By saying the students were the best class in the school | B) By telling the reader to save water at home | C) By reporting results that were checked: the taps stopped dripping and the water bill was lower. | D) By describing the colors of the signs
why correct: The author points to evidence collected “a month later,” which shows a reporting point of view.
tip: Notice whether an author proves a point with facts or with opinions.

passage: Baking Bread in a Clay Oven
stem: What is the author’s main purpose in “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven”?
options / answer: A) To persuade readers to buy bread | B) To tell a funny story about a baker | C) To compare clay ovens with metal ones | D) To explain how bread is baked in a clay oven
why correct: The article walks through the steps of baking.
tip: Ask: Is the author informing, persuading or entertaining?

stem: Why did the author write “Our School Needs a Garden”?
options / answer: A) To persuade the school to build a garden | B) To entertain with a garden adventure | C) To describe a garden that already exists | D) To teach readers how to grow tomatoes
why correct: The author gives reasons why the school “should” build a garden.
tip: “Should” often signals persuasion.

stem: Why does the author of “How Honeybees Share Directions” explain how scientists studied bees?
options / answer: A) To explain how honey is sold | B) To show readers how we know about the bee dances | C) To describe the colors of glass | D) To convince readers to become scientists
why correct: The last paragraph explains the source of the information.
tip: Authors include details for a reason.

stem: Why does the author of “Nature’s Engineers” use headings?
options / answer: A) To show the beaver’s point of view | B) To tell the reader what to believe | C) To organize information so readers can find each part easily | D) To make the article longer
why correct: Headings like “Building a Dam” divide the article into topics.
tip: Text features support the author’s purpose.

stem: The author of “The Dripping Taps” ends with: “a small problem, noticed and measured, can lead to a big change.” What purpose does this ending serve?
options / answer: A) To list the steps the students took | B) To describe the plumber’s job | C) To introduce a new problem | D) To share a lesson readers can use in their own lives
why correct: The final sentence turns the event into a general lesson.
tip: Endings often show the author’s deeper purpose.

stem: In “The Dripping Taps,” what CAUSED the cup to fill?
options / answer: A) Water dripped from the tap. | B) Rain fell into the cup. | C) The students drank the water. | D) The plumber poured water in.
why correct: The dripping tap slowly filled the cup.
tip: A cause is why something happens.

stem: What was one EFFECT of the class’s signs?
options / answer: A) The principal wrote a letter. | B) More students turned off the water while soaping. | C) The cup was placed under the tap. | D) The taps started dripping again.
why correct: Teachers noticed more students turning off the water.
tip: An effect is what happens because of a cause.

stem: Match each cause with its effect.
options / answer: The beaver dam slows the stream = A deep, calm pond forms | The lodge entrances are underwater = Predators cannot easily reach the family | A pond is the only water for miles = Deer and birds travel to drink there
why correct: Each effect in the article is caused by something beavers build.
tip: Look for signal words: because, so, as a result.

passage: Baking Bread in a Clay Oven
stem: In “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven,” why must the oven walls be very hot before the dough is added?
options / answer: A) Hot walls keep insects away from the bread. | B) Hot walls make the clay oven stronger. | C) The bread bakes on the hot wall in only a few minutes. | D) Hot walls help the dough rise under the cloth.
why correct: The bread is pressed onto the wall and puffs up after a few minutes, which needs a very hot surface.
tip: Connect a step to its result.

stem: What is the main idea of “Keeping Bees in the Mountains”?
options / answer: A) Smoke calms bees. | B) Sidr trees grow in mountains. | C) Honey is sold at markets. | D) Mountain families carefully keep bees and collect honey.
why correct: Every paragraph tells about how the families keep bees and make honey.
tip: The main idea covers the whole text.

stem: Which detail BEST supports the main idea of “How Honeybees Share Directions”?
options / answer: A) The direction of the waggle tells bees which way to fly. | B) Bees need food. | C) Hives can have glass walls. | D) Bees live in colonies.
why correct: This detail directly explains how bees share directions.
tip: Supporting details explain the main idea.

stem: What is the central idea of “The Dripping Taps”?
options / answer: A) Principals read letters. | B) Students noticed water being wasted and took steps that saved water. | C) Signs should be bright. | D) Plumbers fix taps.
why correct: The text follows the problem, the actions and the result.
tip: Ask: What is the whole article mostly about?

stem: Which TWO details support the main idea of “Nature’s Engineers”?
options / answer: A) Beavers pile sticks, rocks and mud to build dams. | B) Wolves are predators. | C) Beaver ponds give frogs, ducks and fish a home. | D) Some roads flood.
why correct: The main idea is that beavers change the land and help other living things.
tip: Supporting details connect to the main idea.

passage: Baking Bread in a Clay Oven
stem: Which sentence would BEST end a summary of the central idea of “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven”?
options / answer: A) Clay ovens are found only in villages. | B) Bakers wake up early. | C) Each careful step turns simple ingredients into warm, golden bread. | D) The basket is the most important tool.
why correct: It captures the whole process from ingredients to finished bread.
tip: A central idea ties all the steps together.

stem: Which word BEST describes Omar in “The Stick Bridge”?
options / answer: A) mean | B) careless | C) lazy | D) helpful
why correct: Omar points out the crack and suggests triangles.
tip: Use actions to describe a character.

stem: How does Noura change from the flashback to the present in “The Pearl Diver’s Daughter”?
options / answer: A) She stops fearing the sea but starts fearing time without her father. | B) She stops loving her father. | C) She decides to go pearling. | D) She becomes afraid of the stars.
why correct: At five the waves frightened her; at ten she fears “the empty months without him.”
tip: Compare a character at two times.

stem: What does the grandmother’s way of helping in “The Kite Repair” show about her?
options / answer: A) She prefers new kites to old ones. | B) She teaches by working alongside Omar instead of simply fixing it for him. | C) She thinks Omar is too young to help. | D) She does not care about the festival.
why correct: She brings tape and tissue paper, shares a memory, and they patch the kite “together.”
tip: A character’s methods reveal their values.

stem: Which signal words show compare and contrast?
options / answer: A) because, so, as a result | B) first, next, finally | C) both, however, unlike | D) the problem, the solution
why correct: Compare-contrast texts use words that show likenesses and differences.
tip: Learn the signal words for each structure.

stem: In “How Honeybees Share Directions,” how are the waggle dance and the round dance DIFFERENT?
options / answer: A) Both dances are for food that is very far away. | B) Only the round dance happens inside the hive. | C) The waggle dance is done by scientists. | D) The waggle dance is for far food; the round dance is for nearby food.
why correct: The article contrasts when each dance is used.
tip: Contrast = how things are different.

stem: The last paragraph of “Nature’s Engineers” contrasts the problems beavers cause with their benefits.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: It says dams can flood roads, but scientists argue the benefits are greater.
tip: “However” often signals a contrast.

stem: Match each description of a text with the structure it would use.
options / answer: Steps for baking bread, from mixing to serving = Sequence | Students find wasted water and fix it = Problem and solution | Details about how bees dance = Description | How two kinds of dances are alike and different = Compare and contrast
why correct: Each structure fits a different kind of information.
tip: Ask how the information would best be organized.

stem: Why might an author use a compare-and-contrast structure to write about beaver dams?
options / answer: A) To show the benefits of dams alongside the problems they cause | B) To tell a story about one beaver family | C) To list the steps for building a dam in order | D) To describe only what a lodge looks like
why correct: Comparing benefits and problems helps readers weigh both sides.
tip: Structure should match the author’s purpose.

stem: In a play, what is the list of characters called?
options / answer: A) the caption | B) the cast | C) the stanza | D) the chapter
why correct: Plays begin with a cast list (CHARACTERS).
tip: Drama words: cast, scene, dialogue, stage directions.

stem: What does the stage direction “(KARIM paces back and forth)” show?
options / answer: A) Karim is looking for the ranger. | B) Karim is lost in the dark. | C) Karim is nervous and restless. | D) Karim is calm and relaxed.
why correct: Pacing back and forth often shows worry.
tip: Stage directions show feelings through actions.

stem: How is “The Missing Map” different from a story about the same events?
options / answer: A) It has no characters. | B) It rhymes like a poem. | C) It has no problem. | D) It is told through dialogue and stage directions instead of a narrator.
why correct: Plays show events through what characters say and do on stage.
tip: Drama: dialogue + stage directions.

stem: Why does Ms. Hassan enter near the END of the play?
options / answer: A) To show that Layla solved the problem before any adult arrived | B) To find the map for them | C) To start a new problem | D) To tell them they took the wrong trail
why correct: Her late entrance lets her praise Layla’s “calm head.”
tip: Think about why a character enters at a certain moment.

stem: Which words from “Night Rain” help you HEAR the rain?
options / answer: A) “a shining stream” | B) “tapping on my roof” | C) “my blanket to my chin” | D) “blurry moons”
why correct: Tapping is a sound.
tip: Imagery can appeal to hearing.

stem: In “Night Rain,” what are the “blurry moons”?
options / answer: A) Puddles on the ground | B) Real moons in the sky | C) The street lamps seen through the rain | D) Raindrops on the window
why correct: “The lamps are blurry moons” compares the lamps to moons.
tip: Read the whole line to see what is being compared.

passage: Baking Bread in a Clay Oven
stem: “The bread puffs up and turns golden brown” helps the reader picture the bread baking.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: You can see the bread rising and changing color.
tip: Imagery helps you see changes.

stem: Which sense does “I pull my blanket to my chin” appeal to?
options / answer: A) hearing | B) taste | C) smell | D) touch
why correct: You can feel the blanket being pulled up.
tip: Ask which sense the words use.

stem: How does the imagery in the last stanza of “Night Rain” change the feeling of the poem?
options / answer: A) It makes the rain feel gentle and comforting as the speaker falls asleep. | B) It makes the rain feel loud and frightening. | C) It shows that the rain has stopped. | D) It describes a sunny morning.
why correct: Images like “singing me to sleep” and “soft and silver feet” create a cozy, peaceful feeling.
tip: Notice how images in the final stanza shape the mood.

stem: Why does Omar kick a stone in “The Kite Repair”?
options / answer: A) He is happy about the festival. | B) He is upset that his kite is ruined. | C) He wants to play football. | D) He is cleaning the garden.
why correct: Kicking a stone right after saying “It’s ruined” shows frustration.
tip: Actions show feelings.

stem: What can you infer about Layla in “The Missing Map”?
options / answer: A) She is afraid of the forest. | B) She knows the trail by heart. | C) She stays calm and thinks carefully under pressure. | D) She doesn’t care about getting lost.
why correct: She sits on a rock, studies the sign, and uses the sun and the lake.
tip: Combine clues to understand a character.

stem: In “The Pearl Diver’s Daughter,” the white shell will help Noura feel close to her father.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: He says she will “hear the sea that is carrying me home.”
tip: Use what characters say to make inferences.

stem: Based on “The Dripping Taps,” what can you infer about Mrs. Hassan?
options / answer: A) She was angry with the class. | B) She fixed the taps herself. | C) She ignored the problem. | D) She took the students’ letter seriously.
why correct: After the letter, “the school asked a plumber to fix the leaking taps.”
tip: Inferences use text evidence.

stem: In “The Kite Repair,” why does Omar know “the patch was the strongest part of all”?
options / answer: A) Because fixing it taught him how the kite works, just as his grandmother said | B) Because the patch fell off | C) Because the patch was made of metal | D) Because his grandmother told him the color was best
why correct: The kite flew steadily in strong wind, proving his grandmother’s idea about fixing things.
tip: Connect the ending to earlier dialogue.

stem: What happens FIRST in “The Missing Map”?
options / answer: A) Layla studies the sign. | B) Layla finds that the map is gone. | C) Karim stops pacing. | D) Ms. Hassan enters.
why correct: The play opens with Layla turning her backpack upside down.
tip: Track events from beginning to end.

stem: What is the turning point in “The Kite Repair”?
options / answer: A) The festival is in two days. | B) Omar kicks a stone. | C) Omar and his grandmother patch the kite and lengthen its tail. | D) The wind pushes the kite into the tree.
why correct: Fixing the kite changes the direction of the story.
tip: The turning point changes things for the better or worse.

stem: Put these events from “The Pearl Diver’s Daughter” in the order they are TOLD.
options / answer: Noura walks down to the shore. → Her father asks about her first trip to the shore. → Noura remembers being five. → Her father gives her a white shell. → The dhow sails away.
why correct: The flashback is told in the middle of the story.
tip: Order of telling can differ from order of happening.

stem: Why does the author have the bridge break on Tuesday night instead of during the contest?
options / answer: A) So the teacher can build a new bridge | B) So the contest can be canceled | C) So Maya can quit the contest | D) So Maya and Omar have time to fix it, which leads to a successful ending.
why correct: A break before the contest creates a problem that can still be solved in time.
tip: Authors place events in an order that builds the plot.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: How many lines are in each stanza of “Rain on the Roof”?
options / answer: A) four | B) six | C) two | D) eight
why correct: The poem has two stanzas of four lines each.
tip: A stanza is a group of lines; count one group.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: Which lines in “Rain on the Roof” rhyme?
options / answer: A) glass / slip | B) begins / pins | C) roof / rain | D) clouds / road
why correct: “Begins” and “pins” end with the same sound.
tip: Rhyming words often end lines.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: What is the rhyme pattern of the first stanza of “Night Rain”?
options / answer: A) Lines 1 and 2 rhyme. | B) No lines rhyme. | C) Lines 2 and 4 rhyme (slow/below). | D) Every line rhymes.
why correct: “Slow” (line 2) and “below” (line 4) rhyme.
tip: Mark the last word of each line to find the pattern.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: How is “Night Rain” organized?
options / answer: A) as a numbered list of steps | B) in paragraphs with dialogue | C) as a play with a cast list | D) in short lines grouped into stanzas, with some rhyming line endings
why correct: Poems are organized in lines and stanzas, often with rhyme.
tip: Notice the shape of a text on the page.

stem: Which sentence is written in FIRST person?
options / answer: A) I climbed the tall tree. | B) He climbed the tall tree. | C) They climbed the tall tree. | D) She climbed the tall tree.
why correct: First person uses I, me, my, we.
tip: First person: I/we. Third person: he/she/they.

stem: From what point of view is “Night Rain” told?
options / answer: A) Third person: a narrator describes others. | B) First person: the speaker uses “I” and “my.” | C) From the rain’s point of view. | D) Second person: “you” is used.
why correct: “I pull my blanket to my chin” shows first person.
tip: Look for pronouns.

stem: “The Pearl Diver’s Daughter” is told in third person.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The narrator uses “she” and “her” for Noura.
tip: Third person uses he, she and they.

stem: If “The Kite Repair” were told by the grandmother in first person, what would readers learn?
options / answer: A) Why the wind blew | B) Omar’s secret thoughts | C) Her own memories and thoughts about fixing kites | D) Nothing different
why correct: A first-person narrator shares their own thoughts and memories.
tip: Narrator choice changes what we know.

stem: How would “The Missing Map” feel different if it were told by Karim as a first-person story?
options / answer: A) It would become a poem. | B) The map would be found in the backpack. | C) Layla would no longer be in the story. | D) Readers would hear how worried Karim felt while Layla was thinking.
why correct: Karim paces nervously; as narrator he could tell his feelings directly.
tip: Imagine the story through another character’s eyes.

stem: Which sentence from “The Stick Bridge” shows that the bridge succeeded?
options / answer: A) “The bridge did not even wobble.” | B) “Maya’s face felt hot.” | C) “At twelve seconds, there was a sharp snap.” | D) “By Tuesday night the bridge looked perfect.”
why correct: Not wobbling under the dictionary shows success.
tip: Choose evidence that directly proves the point.

stem: Which detail is evidence that beaver ponds help other animals?
options / answer: A) “Their dams can flood roads.” | B) “Frogs lay eggs in the still water, ducks find food.” | C) “Beavers patch any leaks quickly.” | D) “A beaver family begins by piling sticks.”
why correct: This detail names animals that benefit from ponds.
tip: Evidence must match the idea you are supporting.

stem: Which TWO quotations support the idea that Omar’s grandmother is patient?
options / answer: A) “Omar frowned.” | B) “Together they patched the rip.” | C) “It’s ruined,” Omar said. | D) “She did not say anything at first.”
why correct: She waits quietly, then works alongside him.
tip: Find quotations about the right character.

stem: A student says, “The beekeepers care about their bees.” Which quotation is the STRONGEST evidence?
options / answer: A) “Bees turn the nectar into honey.” | B) “Honey from these mountains is famous for its rich taste.” | C) “They always leave enough honey in the hive for the bees to eat.” | D) “Some families have kept honeybees for generations.”
why correct: Leaving honey for the bees shows concern for their survival.
tip: The best evidence clearly proves the claim.

stem: Which text feature in “Nature’s Engineers” tells what each section is about?
options / answer: A) captions | B) a map | C) a glossary | D) headings
why correct: Headings such as “Building a Dam” name each section.
tip: Headings work like signposts.

stem: Where would you look to find the page about beaver lodges in a long book?
options / answer: A) the index | B) the title page | C) the last sentence | D) the dedication
why correct: The index lists topics alphabetically with page numbers.
tip: Index = at the back; table of contents = at the front.

stem: A diagram of a beaver lodge would MOST help readers understand what?
options / answer: A) the history of beavers | B) how the underwater entrances lead into the lodge | C) how many frogs live in the pond | D) why scientists like beavers
why correct: Diagrams show parts and how they fit together.
tip: Choose the feature that fits the information.

stem: Match each text feature with what it shows.
options / answer: Timeline = events in time order | Map = where places are | Chart = numbers or facts in rows and columns | Bold word = an important vocabulary word
why correct: Each feature presents a different kind of information.
tip: Ask what each feature is best at showing.

stem: Which heading would BEST fit the last paragraph of “Nature’s Engineers”?
options / answer: A) Building a Dam | B) Life Under the Ice | C) Problems and Benefits | D) A Beaver’s Diet
why correct: The paragraph discusses flooding problems and the benefits scientists see.
tip: A good heading names the paragraph’s main topic.

stem: What lesson does Maya learn in “The Stick Bridge”?
options / answer: A) Never enter contests. | B) Bridges are boring. | C) Little brothers are annoying. | D) Listen when someone points out a problem.
why correct: She says, “Next time, I’ll listen when you find a crack.”
tip: A theme is a lesson the character learns.

stem: Which theme does “The Dripping Taps” suggest?
options / answer: A) Taking care of shared resources helps everyone. | B) Water is too expensive to use. | C) Only adults can solve problems. | D) Taps are dangerous.
why correct: The students’ care for the school’s water saved water for everyone.
tip: A theme is a message the text suggests.

stem: Read: “The desert was so arid that no plants grew for miles.” What does arid mean?
options / answer: A) very crowded | B) very dry | C) very cold | D) very noisy
why correct: The clue “no plants grew” shows the land had no water.
tip: Look for clues that explain the word.

stem: The root “tele” means far. What is a telescope?
options / answer: A) a tool for hearing music | B) a tool for measuring heat | C) a tool for seeing things that are far away | D) a tool for writing
why correct: tele (far) + scope (see) = see far.
tip: Combine root meanings.

stem: Match each root with its meaning.
options / answer: bio = life | geo = earth | aqua = water | phon = sound
why correct: These roots appear in many science words.
tip: Think of examples: biology, geography, aquarium, phone.

stem: The Latin root “spect” means look or watch. Which word means “a person who watches an event”?
options / answer: A) conductor | B) translator | C) sculptor | D) spectator
why correct: spect (watch) + -ator (one who) = one who watches.
tip: Find the root, then the suffix.

stem: Using roots, what does “geothermal energy” most likely mean?
