options / answer: A) heat energy that comes from inside the earth | B) sound energy from music | C) energy from water in the ocean | D) energy from living plants
why correct: geo (earth) + therm (heat) = heat from the earth.
tip: Break long words into roots.

stem: What does “it’s raining cats and dogs” mean?
options / answer: A) Pets are playing in the rain. | B) It is raining very hard. | C) It is a little cloudy. | D) Animals are falling from the sky.
why correct: This idiom describes very heavy rain.
tip: Idioms mean something different from their words.

stem: Kareem was “all ears” when the coach announced the team. What does this mean?
options / answer: A) He covered his ears. | B) He had large ears. | C) He listened very carefully. | D) He could not hear.
why correct: “All ears” means paying close attention.
tip: Use the situation to understand an idiom.

stem: What does the adage “The early bird catches the worm” teach?
options / answer: A) Never wake up early. | B) Birds should eat worms. | C) Worms are hard to find. | D) People who start early often succeed.
why correct: The saying encourages getting a head start.
tip: Adages are short sayings with life lessons.

stem: Match each saying with its meaning.
options / answer: Break the ice = start a friendly conversation | Hit the books = study hard | Actions speak louder than words = what you do matters more than what you say | Practice makes perfect = doing something often makes you better
why correct: The first two are idioms; the last two are adages.
tip: Think about when people use each saying.

stem: In “The bat flew out of the cave,” what does bat mean?
options / answer: A) a flying animal | B) a stick for hitting a ball | C) to hit something | D) to blink your eyes
why correct: Something that flies out of a cave is an animal.
tip: Use the rest of the sentence to pick the meaning.

stem: Which sentence uses “light” to mean NOT HEAVY?
options / answer: A) Please light the candle. | B) The empty box was light enough to carry. | C) Turn on the light. | D) The room was full of light.
why correct: An empty box that is easy to carry is not heavy.
tip: Test each meaning in the sentence.

stem: Read: “The coach told the team to stick together.” What does stick mean here?
options / answer: A) to poke | B) to glue | C) stay | D) a piece of wood
why correct: “Stick together” means stay together as a group.
tip: Notice whether the word is a noun or a verb.

stem: In which TWO sentences does “ring” mean a sound?
options / answer: A) I heard the phone ring. | B) She wore a gold ring. | C) The boxers stepped into the ring. | D) The bells ring at noon.
why correct: Phones and bells make sounds.
tip: Group sentences by the meaning used.

stem: Choose the word that means “not tidy”: “Clothes all over the floor made the room ____.”
options / answer: A) tidy | B) retidy | C) tidier | D) untidy
why correct: un- means not: untidy = not tidy, messy.
tip: un- = not.

stem: Choose the word that means “not agree”: “The two friends ____ about the best game.”
options / answer: A) disagree | B) reagree | C) preagree | D) overagree
why correct: dis- means not or opposite: disagree.
tip: dis- = not, opposite of.

stem: What does “overcooked” mean?
options / answer: A) cooked again | B) cooked before | C) not cooked | D) cooked too much
why correct: over- means too much.
tip: over- = too much.

stem: Which word means “not able to be seen”?
options / answer: A) invisible | B) visible | C) revisible | D) previsible
why correct: in- means not: invisible = not able to be seen.
tip: Some prefixes mean “not”: un-, in-, im-, dis-, non-.

stem: What does “teacher” mean?
options / answer: A) the act of teaching | B) one who teaches | C) full of teaching | D) teaching again
why correct: -er can mean “one who.”
tip: -er/-or = one who.

stem: What does “joyful” mean?
options / answer: A) one who brings joy | B) joy again | C) full of joy | D) without joy
why correct: -ful means full of.
tip: -ful = full of.

stem: Choose the word that means “in a quiet way”: “The baby slept ____.”
options / answer: A) quietness | B) quietly | C) quieter | D) quietful
why correct: -ly means “in a … way.”
tip: -ly often makes an adverb.

stem: How does the suffix change the word in “The movement of the ship made me dizzy”?
options / answer: A) -ment means “one who moves.” | B) -ment makes the word mean “not move.” | C) -ment makes the word plural. | D) -ment turns the verb “move” into a noun.
why correct: move (verb) + -ment = movement (noun).
tip: Suffixes can change a word’s part of speech.

stem: Which word is a synonym for “brave”?
options / answer: A) courageous | B) lazy | C) sleepy | D) timid
why correct: Courageous and brave mean almost the same.
tip: Synonyms have similar meanings.

stem: Which word is an antonym for “ancient”?
options / answer: A) old | B) modern | C) dusty | D) historic
why correct: Ancient means very old; modern means new.
tip: Antonyms have opposite meanings.

stem: Match each word with its ANTONYM.
options / answer: ancient = modern | generous = selfish | timid = bold | rough = smooth
why correct: Each pair has opposite meanings.
tip: Think of the opposite meaning first.

stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
options / answer: A) becuase | B) becaus | C) because | D) beacause
why correct: because: b-e-c-a-u-s-e.
tip: Say each part slowly: be-cause.

stem: Add -ed to the word stop: “The bus ____ at the corner.”
options / answer: (typed)
why correct: Double the final consonant before adding -ed: stopped.
tip: Short vowel + one consonant: double it before -ed.

stem: Which sentence has every word spelled correctly?
options / answer: A) We were surprised by the beatiful weather. | B) We were surprised by the beautiful wether. | C) We were suprised by the beautiful weather. | D) We were surprised by the beautiful weather.
why correct: surprised, beautiful and weather are spelled correctly.
tip: Check tricky words letter by letter.

stem: Add -ing to the word make: “I am ____ a card for my mother.”
options / answer: (typed)
why correct: Drop the silent e before adding -ing: making.
tip: Silent e + -ing: drop the e.

stem: Which word is more precise than “said” in: “‘Help!’ he ____.”
options / answer: A) shouted | B) did | C) talked | D) went
why correct: “Shouted” shows how he spoke.
tip: Precise words give clearer pictures.

stem: Which sentence uses the most precise language?
options / answer: A) The dog ate stuff. | B) The golden retriever chewed the red sneaker. | C) The animal did something to the thing. | D) The dog chewed the shoe.
why correct: Specific nouns and details create a clear picture.
tip: Replace general words with specific ones.

stem: Which sentence is the most precise for a science report?
options / answer: A) The water boiled pretty fast. | B) The water did a cool thing. | C) The water boiled at 100 degrees Celsius after eight minutes. | D) The water got really hot after a while.
why correct: Reports use exact numbers and terms.
tip: Use measurements and specific vocabulary in reports.

stem: Which revision of “The big storm made a lot of damage” is MOST precise?
options / answer: A) Something happened during the storm. | B) The storm was really big and bad. | C) The large storm made much damage. | D) The fierce sandstorm tore three palm trees from the ground.
why correct: Specific words (fierce sandstorm, three palm trees, tore) show exactly what happened.
tip: Precise language names exact things, numbers and actions.

stem: Which word is an adverb? “The fox crept silently through the grass.”
options / answer: A) silently | B) fox | C) grass | D) crept
why correct: “Silently” tells how the fox crept.
tip: Adverbs tell how, when, where or how often.

stem: Choose the adverb that tells HOW OFTEN: “Our family ____ eats dinner together.”
options / answer: A) delicious | B) hungry | C) always | D) kitchen
why correct: “Always” tells how often.
tip: Frequency adverbs: always, usually, often, sometimes, never.

stem: Which word does the adverb “almost” describe in “The jar was almost empty”?
options / answer: A) was | B) empty | C) The | D) jar
why correct: “Almost” tells to what extent the jar was empty.
tip: Adverbs can describe adjectives.

stem: Choose the correct form: “Of everyone in the choir, Reem sings ____.”
options / answer: A) clearliest | B) clearest | C) more clearly | D) most clearly
why correct: Comparing many people uses “most” + adverb.
tip: Two → more; three or more → most.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The team played |  real well |  in the |  final match.
why correct: “Really” is the adverb that describes “well”; “real” is an adjective.
tip: Use an adverb to describe another adverb.

stem: Which group of words is a dependent clause?
options / answer: A) We played outside. | B) the heavy rain | C) until the rain stops | D) The rain stopped.
why correct: It has a subject and verb but begins with “until,” so it cannot stand alone.
tip: Subordinating conjunctions make clauses dependent.

stem: What is the independent clause? “Although the test was long, Salma finished early.”
options / answer: A) the test was long | B) Although the test was long | C) finished early | D) Salma finished early
why correct: “Salma finished early” can stand alone.
tip: Remove the clause that starts with although/because/when.

stem: Choose the subordinating conjunction: “Please wait here ____ I get the tickets.”
options / answer: A) while | B) and | C) but | D) so
why correct: “While” makes a dependent clause about time.
tip: Subordinating: while, because, although, unless, until.

stem: Which revision turns two choppy sentences into ONE complex sentence with the clearest meaning? “The museum was closed. We visited the park.”
options / answer: A) Because the museum was closed, we visited the park. | B) The museum was closed and we visited the park. | C) Although we visited the park, the museum was closed. | D) The museum was closed, we visited the park.
why correct: “Because” shows that the closed museum caused the change of plan.
tip: Choose the conjunction that matches the relationship.

stem: Combine: “Hala likes chess. Hala likes painting.”
options / answer: A) Hala likes chess, likes painting. | B) Hala likes chess and painting. | C) Hala likes chess Hala likes painting. | D) Chess and painting likes Hala.
why correct: Join the two objects with “and” and remove repeated words.
tip: Combine words that repeat.

stem: Combine using an appositive: “Dr. Noor is a dentist. Dr. Noor lives next door.”
options / answer: A) Dr. Noor lives next door a dentist. | B) Dr. Noor a dentist lives next door. | C) Dr. Noor, a dentist, lives next door. | D) A dentist lives next door Dr. Noor.
why correct: The appositive “a dentist” renames Dr. Noor and is set off by commas.
tip: Place the appositive right after the noun.

stem: Which is the BEST combined sentence? “The cat jumped. The cat landed on the table. The table was wooden.”
options / answer: A) The cat jumped and the cat landed and the table was wooden. | B) Jumping, landing, wooden, the cat. | C) The cat jumped, it landed, the table was wooden. | D) The cat jumped onto the wooden table.
why correct: One clear sentence keeps all the information without repeating.
tip: Cut repeated words and combine actions.

stem: Combine with a participial phrase: “Ali opened the box. He found a letter.”
options / answer: A) Opening the box, Ali found a letter. | B) Opening the box, a letter was found by Ali. | C) Ali opened the box, found a letter. | D) Ali opening the box found a letter.
why correct: The -ing phrase describes Ali, the subject that follows it.
tip: An introductory phrase must describe the subject right after the comma.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: Walking to school, |  the rain soaked |  my backpack |  and my shoes.
correct: segment 2 →  I got soaked by the rain, including
why correct: The phrase “Walking to school” must describe the person walking, not the rain (dangling modifier).
tip: Check who is doing the action in an introductory phrase.

stem: Choose: “A cheetah is ____ than a horse.”
options / answer: A) more fast | B) faster | C) fastest | D) fast
why correct: Two animals → -er: faster.
tip: Two things: -er; many: -est.

stem: Choose: “Mount Everest is the ____ mountain in the world.”
options / answer: A) most high | B) higher | C) highest | D) high
why correct: Comparing with all mountains → highest.
tip: “In the world” signals a superlative.

stem: Which sentence uses “less” or “fewer” correctly?
options / answer: A) This bag has lesser apples. | B) This bag has fewer apples than that one. | C) This bag has fewer sugar than that one. | D) This bag has less apples than that one.
why correct: Apples can be counted, so “fewer.”
tip: fewer = countable; less = not countable.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: My new bike |  is |  more lighter |  than my old one.
why correct: Use -er OR more, never both.
tip: Do not double comparatives.

stem: Which sentence is correct?
options / answer: A) Of the two essays, Hadi’s is the strongest. | B) Of the two essays, Hadi’s is the more stronger. | C) Of the two essays, Hadi’s is the stronger. | D) Of the two essays, Hadi’s is the most strong.
why correct: When comparing exactly two, use the comparative form.
tip: Two items → comparative, even with “the.”

stem: Which coordinating conjunction can mean “because”? “We hurried home, ____ a storm was coming.”
options / answer: A) but | B) so | C) or | D) for
why correct: “For” gives a reason, like “because.”
tip: FANBOYS: for = reason; so = result.

stem: Which compound sentence is punctuated correctly?
options / answer: A) The phone rang, so Majed answered it. | B) The phone rang so, Majed answered it. | C) The phone rang, Majed answered it. | D) The phone, rang so Majed answered it.
why correct: Comma + coordinating conjunction joins two independent clauses.
tip: Comma before FANBOYS.

stem: Which sentence correctly uses “not only … but also”?
options / answer: A) Hessa not only won the race also broke the record. | B) Hessa not only won the race but also broke the record. | C) Hessa not only won the race but broke also the record. | D) Not only Hessa won the race but also broke the record.
why correct: “Not only won … but also broke” joins two parallel verb phrases.
tip: Correlative pairs join matching parts.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: Which TWO words are common nouns? “The scientist studied the volcano near Naples.”
options / answer: A) scientist | B) volcano | C) Naples | D) studied
why correct: Common nouns name general people, places or things.
tip: Proper nouns are capitalized; common nouns are not.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: Which word is a concrete noun?
options / answer: A) honesty | B) curiosity | C) telescope | D) freedom
why correct: You can see and touch a telescope.
tip: Concrete nouns can be sensed.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: In “My parents walked the dog around the park,” how is “dog” used?
options / answer: A) as the subject | B) as a verb | C) as the object of a preposition | D) as a direct object
why correct: The dog receives the action of “walked.”
tip: A direct object answers “what?” or “whom?” after the verb.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: Which word is the object of a preposition? “The kite drifted over the hills.”
options / answer: A) hills | B) drifted | C) kite | D) over
why correct: “Hills” comes after the preposition “over.”
tip: Preposition + noun = object of the preposition.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: Which sentence uses a collective noun with a singular verb correctly?
options / answer: A) The committee meet every Monday. | B) The committee meets every Monday. | C) The committees meets every Monday. | D) The committee are meeting every Monday.
why correct: A committee acting together is one unit, so the verb is singular.
tip: Collective nouns usually take singular verbs.

stem: Which word is a preposition? “The cat hid behind the sofa.”
options / answer: A) hid | B) cat | C) behind | D) sofa
why correct: “Behind” shows where the cat hid.
tip: Prepositions show position, direction or time.

stem: Choose the preposition of time: “The shop closes ____ midnight.”
options / answer: A) on | B) in | C) over | D) at
why correct: Use “at” with clock times.
tip: at + time; on + day; in + month/year.

stem: What is the prepositional phrase? “Students from every grade joined the parade.”
options / answer: A) every grade joined | B) Students from | C) joined the parade | D) from every grade
why correct: The phrase begins with “from” and ends with the noun “grade.”
tip: Preposition → … → noun.

stem: Which TWO prepositional phrases tell WHERE? “During the trip, we camped beside a lake under the stars.”
options / answer: A) under the stars | B) we camped | C) beside a lake | D) During the trip
why correct: “Beside” and “under” show location.
tip: Ask what each phrase answers: when or where?

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The letter |  was addressed |  to my brother and I |  by mistake.
correct: segment 3 →  to my brother and me
why correct: After the preposition “to,” use the object pronoun “me.”
tip: Objects of prepositions use me, him, her, us, them.

stem: Choose: “The dog wagged ____ tail.”
options / answer: A) its | B) its’ | C) it is | D) it’s
why correct: “Its” shows the tail belongs to the dog.
tip: its = belonging to it.

stem: Choose: “Please put your shoes over ____.”
options / answer: A) they’re | B) there | C) their | D) thier
why correct: “There” names a place.
tip: there contains “here”: it is about place.

stem: Choose: “____ been to the new science museum?”
options / answer: A) Who | B) Whos | C) Who’s | D) Whose
why correct: Who’s = who has.
tip: who’s = who is / who has.

stem: Match each word with its meaning.
options / answer: its = belonging to it | it’s = it is | their = belonging to them | they’re = they are
why correct: Contractions have apostrophes; possessive pronouns do not.
tip: Expand each word to test it.

stem: Which sentence is correct?
options / answer: A) You’re welcome to borrow your cousin’s bike. | B) You’re welcome to borrow you’re cousin’s bike. | C) Your welcome to borrow your cousin’s bike. | D) Your welcome to borrow you’re cousin’s bike.
why correct: You’re = you are; your = belonging to you.
tip: Check each one by expanding it.

stem: Which word is a pronoun? “They planted three trees.”
options / answer: A) trees | B) They | C) planted | D) three
why correct: “They” replaces the names of people.
tip: Pronouns replace nouns.

stem: Choose the possessive pronoun: “The blue umbrella is ____.”
options / answer: A) she | B) herself | C) her’s | D) hers
why correct: “Hers” shows ownership.
tip: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs.

stem: Choose the reflexive pronoun: “I taught ____ to juggle.”
options / answer: A) myself | B) me | C) meself | D) mine
why correct: Reflexive pronouns refer back to the subject.
tip: -self / -selves.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: Each of the boys |  brought |  their own |  lunch.
why correct: “Each” is singular, so the pronoun should be singular: his.
tip: Pronouns agree in number with their antecedents.

stem: Which sentence has a clear pronoun reference?
options / answer: A) Lina told Sara that she won. | B) They gave them a gift. | C) When Lina met Sara, Lina gave her a gift. | D) When Lina met Sara, she gave her a gift.
why correct: Naming Lina again removes the confusion.
tip: Make sure each pronoun clearly points to one noun.

stem: Choose the past progressive: “At eight o’clock, we ____ dinner.”
options / answer: A) will eat | B) were eating | C) have eaten | D) eat
why correct: Past progressive = was/were + -ing.
tip: Progressive tenses show ongoing action.

stem: Which sentence uses the future perfect tense?
options / answer: A) I have finished the book. | B) I am finishing the book. | C) I finished the book in June. | D) By June, I will have finished the book.
why correct: will have + past participle = future perfect.
tip: Perfect tenses use has/have/had/will have.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Choose the LINKING verb: “After the long race, Omar ____ exhausted.”
options / answer: A) jumped | B) ran | C) felt | D) quickly
why correct: “Felt” links Omar to the word that describes him, “exhausted.”
tip: Linking verbs: is, seem, feel, become, look, appear.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Choose the helping verb: “The guests ____ arriving soon.”
options / answer: A) was | B) is | C) has | D) will be
why correct: “Will be arriving” is a verb phrase showing the future.
tip: Helping verb + main verb = verb phrase.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Which sentence has a transitive verb (an action done TO something)?
options / answer: A) Huda painted a mural. | B) Huda arrived early. | C) Huda laughed. | D) Huda seemed tired.
why correct: “Painted” acts on the object “a mural.”
tip: Transitive verbs have a direct object.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Choose the modal that shows ability: “I ____ swim across the pool now.”
options / answer: A) can | B) should | C) must | D) may
why correct: “Can” shows ability.
tip: can = able; must = required; should = advised.

skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs
stem: Which TWO sentences use a verb phrase with a helping verb?
options / answer: A) We are reading a mystery. | B) We read a mystery. | C) The team has practiced every day. | D) The team practiced yesterday.
why correct: has practiced and are reading each contain a helping verb.
tip: Look for has/have/is/are/will before the main verb.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: Yes |  Mr. Salem, |  the report |  is ready.
why correct: A comma follows the introductory word “Yes.” (The comma after the name is already correct.)
tip: Introductory words and direct address both need commas.

stem: Which is the abbreviation for “Street”?
options / answer: A) st | B) St. | C) Str | D) ST
why correct: Street → St.
tip: Address abbreviations: St., Ave., Rd.

stem: How should a song title be written?
options / answer: A) underlined | B) in all capital letters | C) in quotation marks | D) with no marks
why correct: Short works (songs, poems, articles) use quotation marks.
tip: Short works → quotation marks.

stem: Which sentence writes a magazine title and an article title correctly?
options / answer: A) I read Saving the Reefs in “Ocean World.” | B) I read Saving The Reefs in ocean world. | C) I read “saving the reefs” in Ocean World. | D) I read “Saving the Reefs” in Ocean World.
why correct: Article titles take quotation marks; magazine titles are italicized.
tip: Part → quotes; whole → italics.

stem: Which date uses abbreviations correctly?
options / answer: A) Mon., Sept. 7 | B) MON., SEPT. 7 | C) mon., sept. 7 | D) Mon Sept 7
why correct: Abbreviated days and months keep a capital letter and take a period.
tip: Mon., Tues., Jan., Feb.

stem: Which sentence is correct?
options / answer: A) Dr Hamid’s book, “The Desert Garden,” won an award. | B) Dr. Hamid’s book, The Desert Garden, won an award. | C) Dr. Hamid’s book, the Desert Garden, won an award. | D) dr. Hamid’s book, The desert garden, won an award.
why correct: Title abbreviation with a period; book title italicized with capitals.
tip: Check abbreviation, marks and capitals.

stem: What is the main purpose of “Why the Moon Changes Shape”?
options / answer: A) to tell a story about astronauts | B) to describe how calendars are printed | C) to explain why the Moon looks different during the month | D) to persuade readers to visit space
why correct: The article explains moon phases.
tip: Ask: inform, persuade or entertain?

stem: Why does the author of “Catching Water in the Desert” begin by describing rare rain?
options / answer: A) to describe a holiday | B) to explain how clouds form | C) to complain about the weather | D) to show the problem that the solutions address
why correct: The opening sets up the problem of saving water.
tip: Openings often introduce the problem or topic.

stem: How is the purpose of the news report different from Rania’s journal in “The Storm: Two Accounts”?
options / answer: A) The report informs with facts; the journal shares personal feelings. | B) The journal gives exact rainfall. | C) Both mainly share feelings. | D) The report is fiction.
why correct: The report lists wind speeds and outages; the journal says “I was scared.”
tip: Compare purpose through the details each writer chooses.

passage: Sea Turtles of the Red Sea
stem: Why does the turtle article include a glossary?
options / answer: A) to list every turtle species | B) to help readers understand a key word | C) to tell a story | D) to persuade readers to protect turtles
why correct: The glossary defines “hatchling.”
tip: Text features support the author’s purpose.

stem: The author of “Catching Water in the Desert” ends with engineers combining ancient ideas and modern materials. What point of view does this ending suggest?
options / answer: A) Modern materials make ancient ideas useless. | B) Engineers should stop using cisterns. | C) Old solutions are still valuable and can be improved, not replaced. | D) Desert farming is impossible.
why correct: The final sentence shows respect for ancient methods and hope for improvement.
tip: Endings often reveal the author’s attitude.

stem: In “Catching Water in the Desert,” what causes rainwater to disappear quickly?
options / answer: A) Cisterns leak. | B) Check dams block it. | C) People drink it immediately. | D) It rushes over hard, dry ground.
why correct: The text says water “rushes over the hard, dry ground and disappears.”
tip: Find what makes something happen.

stem: What is an effect of check dams?
options / answer: A) Water soaks into the soil instead of running away. | B) Rain falls more often. | C) The ground becomes harder. | D) Cisterns become larger.
why correct: The walls slow the water, “giving it time to soak into the soil.”
tip: Signal words like “giving” can show effects.

stem: In “The Storm: Two Accounts,” what was an effect of the 120 millimeters of rain?
options / answer: A) Winds of 90 kilometers per hour | B) Flooding on six streets | C) Power restored by noon | D) Lightning at 3 a.m.
why correct: Heavy rain in six hours flooded streets.
tip: Connect each cause with its direct result.

passage: Sea Turtles of the Red Sea
stem: Match each cause from the turtle article with its effect.
options / answer: Warmer sand in the nest = More hatchlings become females | Bright lights from buildings = Hatchlings crawl the wrong way | Eggs stay warm for about two months = Hatchlings dig their way out
why correct: Each effect in the article follows from a condition on the beach.
tip: Use “because” to test each pair.

stem: What is the central idea of “Why the Moon Changes Shape”?
options / answer: A) Calendars were invented by farmers. | B) Full moons happen every week. | C) The Moon’s shape seems to change because we see different amounts of its lit half. | D) The Moon makes its own light.
why correct: Every paragraph explains our changing view of the lit half.
tip: The central idea connects all paragraphs.

passage: Sea Turtles of the Red Sea
stem: Which detail BEST supports the central idea of the turtle article?
options / answer: A) Hatchling is defined in the glossary. | B) The Red Sea is warm. | C) A caption describes a photo. | D) Females lay about one hundred eggs on sandy beaches.
why correct: The article is about how Red Sea turtles nest and the dangers hatchlings face.
tip: Supporting details develop the main idea.

stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of “The Last Repair”?
options / answer: A) Under pressure, Khalid succeeds by remembering to slow down. | B) Captains need pocket watches. | C) Jeddah smells of sea salt and cardamom. | D) Uncle Faris has a fever.
why correct: The story turns on Khalid calming himself and finding the spring.
tip: Ask what the whole story is mostly about.

stem: Which word BEST describes Dana in “The Second Try”?
options / answer: A) jealous | B) supportive | C) bored | D) rude
why correct: She whispers encouragement and gives advice.
tip: Use dialogue to describe a character.

stem: How does Salma solve the problem in “The Two Wells”?
options / answer: A) She buys water from Hamdan. | B) She leaves the village. | C) She observes carefully and leads the children to dig a new well. | D) She asks the king for help.
why correct: She notices the green grove and digs there.
tip: Characters’ actions show their traits.

passage: The Volcano That Would Not Erupt
stem: What does Yusuf’s question about the baking soda show about him?
options / answer: A) He forgot the vinegar. | B) He wants to blame Layla. | C) He has given up. | D) He thinks logically when something goes wrong.
why correct: Instead of panicking, he checks the steps.
tip: Problem-solving shows character.

stem: How does Khalid change between the moment the spring disappears and the end of “The Last Repair”?
options / answer: A) He moves from panic to calm, careful action. | B) He gives up and asks the captain for help. | C) He stays panicked until the end. | D) He moves from calm to anger.
why correct: He knocks screws over in panic, then counts to ten and searches slowly.
tip: Track how a character’s behavior changes.

stem: What topic do both accounts in “The Storm: Two Accounts” describe?
options / answer: A) a school play | B) the same storm on March 12 | C) a car accident | D) two different storms
why correct: Both are dated March 12 and describe the storm.
tip: Find the shared topic first.

stem: Which detail appears in BOTH accounts?
options / answer: A) Rania hid in her sister’s bed. | B) Electricity returned by noon. | C) There was flooding in the streets. | D) Winds reached 90 kilometers per hour.
why correct: Rania says the street was a river; the report says six streets flooded.
tip: Look for facts both writers mention.

passage: Two Articles: A School Garden and Red Sea Turtles
stem: Using BOTH articles in the paired passage, which statement is true?
options / answer: A) Both are stories. | B) Both argue for protecting turtles. | C) Both use headings. | D) One argues for gardens with reasons; the other explains facts about turtles with headings.
why correct: The texts differ in purpose and structure.
tip: Compare purpose and structure across texts.

stem: A student writes a report about the storm’s effect on families. Why is using BOTH accounts better than using one?
options / answer: A) The report gives exact facts, and the journal shows how it felt to live through it. | B) The report describes Rania’s fear. | C) Both say the same thing. | D) The journal has more numbers.
why correct: Combining facts and personal experience gives a fuller picture.
tip: Different sources add different kinds of information.

stem: Why does the narrator of “The Second Try” leave the note cards in the desk?
options / answer: A) Because the teacher took them | B) To speak naturally instead of reading | C) Because they were wet | D) Because the cards were lost
why correct: Dana advised, “Just talk like you’re telling me.”
tip: Link actions to earlier advice.

stem: What can you infer about Hamdan at the start of “The Two Wells”?
options / answer: A) He is generous. | B) He dislikes water. | C) He cares more about money than about his neighbors. | D) He is poor.
why correct: He charges a silver coin even as poor families go thirsty.
tip: Actions reveal values.

stem: In “The Last Repair,” the captain is pleased with Khalid’s work.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: “The captain’s smile told him everything.”
tip: Facial expressions support inferences.

stem: Why did the news report most likely include “No injuries were reported”?
options / answer: A) To show the storm was weak | B) To describe Rania’s family | C) To blame the city | D) To reassure readers that no one was hurt
why correct: Reports often include safety information readers want.
tip: Think about what readers need to know.

stem: In “City Morning,” why does the speaker say “That minute, friend, is mine”?
options / answer: A) The speaker treasures a quiet moment before the busy day. | B) The speaker is late for work. | C) The speaker owns the city. | D) The speaker dislikes friends.
why correct: The last stanza contrasts the quiet golden sky with the loud day.
tip: Read the final lines in context.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: How many stanzas are in “Harbor at Dawn”?
options / answer: A) one | B) two | C) eight | D) three
why correct: There are two groups of four lines.
tip: Stanzas are separated by blank lines.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: Which pair of words rhymes in “Harbor at Dawn”?
options / answer: A) boats / wet | B) ropes / breeze | C) light / night | D) gulls / thread
why correct: “Light” and “night” end lines 1 and 2 and rhyme.
tip: Check line endings.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: What is the rhyme pattern of “Harbor at Dawn”?
options / answer: A) only the last line | B) no rhyme at all | C) every other line | D) rhyming pairs (couplets)
why correct: light/night, thread/red, knees/breeze, wet/net.
tip: Couplets: two rhyming lines in a row.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: In “City Morning,” how does the sentence run from stanza 2 into stanza 3?
options / answer: A) The question continues across the stanza break. | B) Stanza 3 repeats stanza 2. | C) The poem has no punctuation. | D) Each stanza is a separate sentence.
why correct: “don’t you miss / The quiet way…” carries the thought into stanza 3 (enjambment).
tip: Lines and stanzas can continue a sentence.

skill: Poetry: Structure, Rhyme, Meter and Form
stem: How does the structure of “Harbor at Dawn” support its meaning?
options / answer: A) The stanzas are numbered steps in a process. | B) Two short rhyming stanzas move from the sky to the boats, like a scene slowly waking. | C) Each stanza tells a different character’s story. | D) It has no stanzas.
why correct: Stanza 1 shows sky and town; stanza 2 the harbor sounds and boats waking.
tip: Ask how form and meaning work together.

stem: From what point of view is “The Two Wells” told?
options / answer: A) Salma’s first person | B) second person | C) third person | D) first person
why correct: The narrator uses she, he and they.
tip: Pronouns reveal point of view.

stem: How does Rania’s first-person journal affect what readers learn?
options / answer: A) Readers learn the officials’ plans. | B) Readers learn exact wind speeds. | C) Readers learn every family’s story. | D) Readers learn her personal feelings, like fear and amazement.
why correct: First person shares the narrator’s inner thoughts.
tip: Narrator choice shapes information.

passage: The Volcano That Would Not Erupt
stem: If “The Volcano That Would Not Erupt” were told by Ms. Dawood, what might change?
options / answer: A) We would see the scene from the teacher’s view, perhaps without knowing about the missing baking soda. | B) The science fair would be canceled. | C) Layla would disappear. | D) The volcano would be made of metal.
why correct: A different narrator knows and notices different things.
tip: Imagine the story through another character.

stem: What is the solution in “The Two Wells”?
options / answer: A) Hamdan builds a wall. | B) The children dig a new well. | C) The village moves. | D) Families go thirsty.
why correct: The new well gives free water.
tip: Solution = what fixes the problem.

passage: Sea Turtles of the Red Sea
stem: In the turtle article, the author gives a full solution for the problem of bright lights.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: The section explains the danger but does not describe a solution.
tip: Not every problem in a text is solved.

stem: How do cisterns and check dams solve the SAME problem in different ways?
options / answer: A) Both pump water from wells. | B) Cisterns are for animals only. | C) Cisterns store water in tanks; check dams help water soak into the ground. | D) Both make it rain more.
why correct: Both save scarce rainwater, using storage or soil.
tip: Compare how two solutions work.

stem: Why does the author of the garden letter offer starting small with containers?
options / answer: A) To show gardens are useless | B) To make gardens larger | C) To save time on reading | D) To solve the problem that gardens may cost too much
why correct: This answers the cost objection with a practical solution.
tip: Persuasive texts can include solutions to objections.

stem: In “The Last Repair,” what happens right after the spring disappears?
options / answer: A) Khalid knocks a box of screws to the floor. | B) He closes the case. | C) He finds the spring. | D) The captain leaves the watch.
why correct: His panic follows immediately.
tip: Track time order.

stem: Put the steps of collecting rainwater in a cistern in order.
options / answer: Rain falls on the rooftop. → Gutters guide the water into pipes. → Pipes lead the water to the cistern. → The covered tank keeps the water cool.
why correct: The article describes the path from roof to tank.
tip: Follow the path of the water.

stem: Put the events in the news report in time order.
options / answer: The storm strikes early Thursday morning. → Streets flood and power goes out. → City crews begin clearing drains at 7 a.m. → Electricity is restored by noon.
why correct: The report moves from the storm to the recovery.
tip: Use times as clues.

stem: After a full moon, what happens next in the cycle described in the article?
options / answer: A) The Moon stops reflecting light. | B) The pattern reverses until the next new moon. | C) A full moon happens again the next night. | D) The Moon becomes a crescent immediately.
why correct: The article says, “Then the pattern reverses until the next new moon.”
tip: Cycles return to their starting point.

stem: Which line from “City Morning” uses onomatopoeia?
options / answer: A) “The city yawns and stretches wide,” | B) “Above the rooftop line?” | C) “The coffee kettles hiss;” | D) “That minute, friend, is mine.”
why correct: “Hiss” imitates a sound.
tip: Onomatopoeia = sound words.

stem: Which words in “Harbor at Dawn” show alliteration?
options / answer: A) “fishing boats, still beaded wet” | B) “the last stars folding up the night” | C) “the bread oven breathes” | D) “salt and diesel… stitch the sky with silver”
why correct: Many words repeat the s sound: stitch, sky, silver, salt.
tip: Listen for repeated beginning sounds.

stem: Which sound device appears in “Ropes creak”?
options / answer: A) onomatopoeia | B) repetition | C) alliteration | D) rhyme
why correct: “Creak” imitates the sound of ropes.
tip: Sound words imitate real sounds.

stem: Match each example from “City Morning” with its sound device.
options / answer: hiss = Onomatopoeia | busy, bustling, buzzing = Alliteration | wide / side = Rhyme
why correct: Each example uses sound in a different way.
tip: Say each aloud.

stem: Why does the poet use the alliteration “busy, bustling, buzzing throng”?
options / answer: A) To make the poem rhyme | B) The repeated b sounds create a noisy, rushing feeling like a crowd. | C) To describe silence | D) To slow the poem down
why correct: The fast repeated b sounds echo the energy of the crowd.
tip: Sound devices support meaning.

stem: Which sentence shows that the narrator of “The Second Try” was nervous at first?
options / answer: A) “Dana leaned over.” | B) “Heads lifted.” | C) “My hands shook.” | D) “I was smiling.”
why correct: Shaking hands show nervousness.
tip: Choose evidence that directly shows the idea.

stem: Which sentence supports the idea that cisterns are an old invention?
options / answer: A) “Farmers build low walls of earth.” | B) “Rain falls only a few times each year.” | C) “Gutters on rooftops guide rainwater.” | D) “Archaeologists have found cisterns that are more than two thousand years old.”
why correct: Two-thousand-year-old cisterns prove they are ancient.
tip: Match evidence to the claim.

stem: Which evidence shows that the villagers valued sharing?
options / answer: A) “they shared it freely, as they always had.” | B) “every bucket costs a silver coin.” | C) “Hamdan’s gate stayed locked.” | D) “Their hands blistered.”
why correct: The villagers choose to share the new well freely.
tip: Quote words that prove the point.

stem: Which TWO quotations support the idea that the storm was serious?
options / answer: A) “No injuries were reported.” | B) “winds of up to 90 kilometers per hour” | C) “power outages affecting about 4,000 homes” | D) “electricity was restored to most homes by noon.”
why correct: High winds and many outages show a serious storm.
tip: Choose evidence that fits the claim.

passage: The Volcano That Would Not Erupt
stem: A student claims, “Layla learned from her mistake.” Which quotation is the STRONGEST evidence?
options / answer: A) “The judges come at ten o’clock.” | B) “You check every step, and you never panic.” | C) “Everything is ruined!” | D) “The baking soda… is still in my backpack.”
why correct: Her final line states what she learned.
tip: The best evidence directly proves the claim.

stem: What is a theme of “The Two Wells”?
options / answer: A) Deserts are hot. | B) Children should not dig. | C) Sharing is worth more than profit. | D) Merchants are always kind.
why correct: Hamdan admits shared water is worth more than sold water.
tip: Theme = message about life.

stem: Which detail BEST supports the theme of “The Last Repair”?
options / answer: A) “Uncle Faris had a fever.” | B) “The ship’s horn sounded.” | C) “The narrow lanes smelled of sea salt.” | D) “A watchmaker’s hands must be slower than the sand.”
why correct: The uncle’s lesson about patience is the message of the story.
tip: Find the line that states the lesson.

passage: The Volcano That Would Not Erupt
stem: What theme does “The Volcano That Would Not Erupt” express?
options / answer: A) Staying calm and checking your work helps you solve problems. | B) Partners always cause problems. | C) Science fairs are unfair. | D) Volcanoes are dangerous.
why correct: Layla’s last line states the lesson: check every step and never panic.
tip: A theme is a message about life.

stem: How does the turtle memory in “The Second Try” help develop the theme?
options / answer: A) It explains how to give a speech. | B) The turtles keep going after being knocked back, just as the narrator does. | C) It shows turtles are dangerous. | D) It distracts from the story.
why correct: “Being knocked back… isn’t the same as being beaten.”
tip: Symbols and memories can carry themes.

stem: Read: “The puppy was so lethargic after the long walk that it slept all afternoon.” What does lethargic mean?
options / answer: A) very excited | B) very loud | C) very tired and slow | D) very hungry
why correct: The clue “slept all afternoon” shows tiredness.
tip: Use the effect described in the sentence.

stem: Read: “Unlike his loquacious cousin, who chatted for hours, Tamer rarely spoke more than a few words.” What does loquacious mean?
options / answer: A) very quiet | B) very rude | C) very tall | D) very talkative
why correct: The contrast word “Unlike” and “chatted for hours” show the meaning.
tip: Contrast clues show the opposite of a nearby word.

stem: “The baker sings a sugared song.” What kind of figurative language describes the song as “sugared”?
options / answer: A) a metaphor suggesting the song is sweet | B) a simile using “like” | C) a literal description | D) onomatopoeia
why correct: The song is described as if it were sweet like sugar.
tip: Metaphors compare without like or as.

stem: In “Harbor at Dawn,” what does “The harbor yawns” suggest?
options / answer: A) The harbor is bored. | B) The harbor is just waking up, like a sleepy person. | C) The harbor is wide open and empty forever. | D) The harbor makes a loud noise.
why correct: Personification gives the harbor a human action at dawn.
tip: Personification gives human traits to things.

stem: The Latin root “aqua” means water. Which word names a tank for fish?
options / answer: A) terrarium | B) auditorium | C) aquarium | D) planetarium
why correct: aqua (water) + -arium (place) = aquarium.
tip: Roots carry the core meaning.

stem: The Greek root “chron” means time. What is a chronological list?
options / answer: A) a list of colors | B) a list in alphabetical order | C) a list in size order | D) a list in time order
why correct: chron (time) → in the order things happened.
tip: Think of chronicle, chronometer.

stem: Using roots, what does “benevolent” most likely mean?
options / answer: A) wishing to do good for others | B) wishing harm on others | C) able to fly | D) very strong
why correct: bene (good) + vol (wish) = wishing good.
tip: Combine root meanings to define new words.

stem: Choose the correct word: “The hikers walked for an ____.”
options / answer: A) ower | B) hour | C) are | D) our
why correct: “Hour” means sixty minutes.
tip: Homophones sound alike but differ in meaning.

stem: In which sentence does “lead” rhyme with “bed”?
options / answer: A) Please lead the line to lunch. | B) The pencil’s lead broke during the test. | C) Who will lead the team? | D) The guide will lead us up the trail.
why correct: Lead (the metal or pencil core) rhymes with bed.
tip: Homographs can have different pronunciations.

stem: “The farm was used to produce produce.” How do the two words differ?
options / answer: A) They are spelled differently. | B) Both are nouns. | C) The first is a verb (make); the second is a noun (fruits and vegetables), with different stress. | D) They mean the same thing.
why correct: pro-DUCE (verb) vs. PRO-duce (noun).
tip: Stress can change with part of speech.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The principle |  announced that |  the school |  would close early.
why correct: A principal is the head of a school; a principle is a rule or belief.
tip: Principal = a pal who leads the school.

stem: What does “under the weather” mean?
options / answer: A) checking the forecast | B) very happy | C) standing in the rain | D) feeling sick
why correct: “Under the weather” means feeling unwell.
tip: Idioms are not literal.

stem: Maryam “spilled the beans” about the surprise party. What did she do?
options / answer: A) She told the secret. | B) She hid the gifts. | C) She cooked dinner. | D) She dropped food.
why correct: To spill the beans is to reveal a secret.
tip: Use context to understand idioms.

stem: Match each proverb with its meaning.
options / answer: Look before you leap = think carefully before acting | Many hands make light work = working together makes jobs easier | Don’t judge a book by its cover = don’t judge by appearances | Better late than never = doing something late is better than not doing it
why correct: Proverbs share advice about life.
tip: Think of a situation where each applies.

stem: Choose the word that means “not possible”: “Climbing that cliff without ropes is ____.”
options / answer: A) repossible | B) possibly | C) impossible | D) unpossible
why correct: im- means not: impossible = not possible.
tip: Before p, b or m, “not” is often spelled im-.

stem: Choose the word that means “to spell wrongly”: “Be careful not to ____ the new words.”
options / answer: A) unspell | B) prespell | C) respell | D) misspell
why correct: mis- means wrongly.
tip: mis- = wrongly.

stem: What does “nonfiction” mean?
options / answer: A) writing about the future | B) writing that is not made up | C) writing that is made up | D) poems
why correct: non- means not: not fiction.
tip: non- = not.

stem: Match each prefix with its meaning.
options / answer: pre- = before | dis- = opposite of | over- = too much | non- = not
why correct: Prefixes change the meaning of base words.
tip: Use example words: preview, disagree, overflow, nonstop.

stem: Which word means “to judge someone before knowing them”?
options / answer: A) misjudge | B) rejudge | C) prejudge | D) unjudge
why correct: pre- (before) + judge = judge beforehand.
tip: Choose the prefix that matches the meaning.

stem: Which word is a synonym for “shout”?
options / answer: A) listen | B) sing | C) whisper | D) yell
why correct: Shout and yell both mean to speak very loudly.
tip: Synonyms = similar meanings.

stem: Which word is an antonym for “visible”?
options / answer: A) hidden | B) clear | C) seen | D) bright
why correct: Visible means able to be seen; hidden means not seen.
tip: Antonyms = opposites.

stem: Which word is the BEST synonym for “furious”?
options / answer: A) calm | B) enraged | C) tired | D) annoyed
why correct: Furious and enraged both mean extremely angry.
tip: Match the strength of the feeling.

stem: Match each word with its SYNONYM.
options / answer: swift = fast | ancient = old | courageous = brave | gigantic = huge
why correct: Each pair has a similar meaning.
tip: Synonyms can replace each other in a sentence.

stem: Which pair shows antonyms with the strongest contrast?
options / answer: A) cold / chilly | B) warm / cool | C) scorching / freezing | D) hot / warm
why correct: Scorching and freezing are extreme opposites.
tip: Antonyms can show degrees of contrast.

stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
options / answer: A) naybor | B) nieghbor | C) neighbour | D) neighbor
why correct: neighbor: n-e-i-g-h-b-o-r.
tip: Weigh and neighbor: ei says long a.

stem: Add -ly to happy: “The children played ____.”
options / answer: (typed)
why correct: Change y to i before adding -ly: happily.
tip: Consonant + y → i before a suffix.

stem: Which sentence has every word spelled correctly?
options / answer: A) Our committee will definitely receive the separate reports. | B) Our comittee will definitely receive the separate reports. | C) Our committee will definitely recieve the seperate reports. | D) Our committee will definately receive the separate reports.
why correct: committee, definitely, receive, separate are tricky words spelled correctly.
tip: Check commonly misspelled words carefully.

stem: Which word is more precise than “walked” in: “The tired hiker ____ up the hill”?
options / answer: A) did | B) trudged | C) moved | D) went
why correct: “Trudged” shows slow, heavy walking.
tip: Choose verbs that show how.

stem: Which sentence uses the most precise language?
options / answer: A) The bird did a thing. | B) The bird moved fast. | C) The hawk swooped down and snatched a lizard from the rock. | D) The bird went down and got something.
why correct: Specific nouns (hawk, lizard) and verbs (swooped, snatched) create a clear picture.
tip: Replace general words with exact ones.

stem: Which domain-specific word fits a science report? “The water turned into vapor through ____.”
options / answer: A) disappearing | B) going away | C) magic | D) evaporation
why correct: Evaporation is the scientific term.
tip: Use subject-specific vocabulary in reports.

stem: Which revision is MOST precise for a report? “A lot of people came to the event.”
options / answer: A) About 1,200 visitors attended the science fair. | B) Many people came. | C) People came to the thing. | D) Tons of people came to the event.
why correct: Exact numbers and specific nouns make writing precise.
tip: Replace “a lot” with a number.

stem: Which sentence uses precise language to create a formal tone?
options / answer: A) They put off the meeting ’cause of the storm thing. | B) The committee postponed the meeting because of the sandstorm warning. | C) The meeting got moved, like, later. | D) Stuff happened, so no meeting.
why correct: Precise verbs (postponed) and nouns (sandstorm warning) suit formal writing.
tip: Formal writing avoids slang.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which word describes the noun “camel” in “The patient camel waited in the shade”?
options / answer: A) shade | B) waited | C) patient | D) The
why correct: “Patient” tells what kind of camel.
tip: Adjectives describe nouns.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Which sentence uses a predicate adjective?
options / answer: A) The cool air arrived after sunset. | B) We watched the sunset. | C) Sunset came quickly. | D) The desert air felt cool after sunset.
why correct: “Cool” follows the linking verb “felt” and describes the subject.
tip: Predicate adjectives follow linking verbs.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Choose the correct form: “Of the two routes, the coastal road is ____.”
options / answer: A) more scenic | B) scenicer | C) most scenic | D) more scenicer
why correct: Comparing exactly two routes: more scenic.
tip: Two → comparative; three+ → superlative.

skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives
stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: She bought |  a new, wooden, |  jewelry box |  in the souq.
why correct: No comma between adjectives that are not coordinate (you would not say “new and wooden jewelry box” naturally), and never a comma before the noun.
tip: Use commas only between coordinate adjectives, and never before the noun.

stem: Which clause is dependent? “Unless the bus arrives soon, we will be late.”
options / answer: A) Unless the bus arrives soon | B) the bus arrives | C) we will be late | D) we will
why correct: “Unless” makes the clause dependent.
tip: Dependent clauses begin with subordinating conjunctions or relative pronouns.

stem: Which sentence contains a relative clause?
options / answer: A) The coach retired, and we were sad. | B) The coach who trained us retired this year. | C) The coach retired this year. | D) Because the coach retired, we were sad.
why correct: “who trained us” describes the coach.
tip: Relative clauses begin with who, which, that, whose.

stem: Choose the relative pronoun: “The book ____ cover is torn belongs to the library.”
options / answer: A) which | B) whose | C) that | D) who’s
why correct: “Whose” shows the cover belongs to the book.
tip: whose = possession.

stem: Which sentence is compound-complex?
options / answer: A) We lit candles. | B) We lit candles, and Mariam told stories. | C) When the power failed, we lit candles, and Mariam told stories. | D) When the power failed, we lit candles.
why correct: It has two independent clauses and one dependent clause.
tip: Compound-complex = 2+ independent + 1+ dependent.

stem: Which revision places the relative clause correctly to avoid confusion?
options / answer: A) That my aunt made, the vase sat on the shelf. | B) The vase sat that my aunt made on the shelf. | C) The vase sat on the shelf that my aunt made. | D) The vase that my aunt made sat on the shelf.
why correct: A relative clause should sit right after the noun it describes.
tip: Place modifiers next to what they modify.

stem: Which is a fragment?
options / answer: A) Because the robotics club stayed late. | B) Yusuf missed the bus. | C) The robotics club stayed late. | D) He walked home.
why correct: A dependent clause alone is a fragment.
tip: Ask: Because… what happened?

stem: Which is a comma splice?
options / answer: A) The reef is fragile, so it needs protection. | B) The reef is fragile, it needs protection. | C) The reef is fragile. | D) The reef is fragile; it needs protection.
why correct: Two independent clauses joined only by a comma form a comma splice.
tip: Comma alone ≠ enough to join sentences.

stem: Which revision fixes the run-on? “Scientists grow corals in nurseries they transplant them to reefs.”
options / answer: A) Scientists grow corals in nurseries, they transplant them to reefs. | B) Scientists grow corals. In nurseries they transplant them to reefs. | C) Scientists grow corals in nurseries; then they transplant them to reefs. | D) Scientists grow corals in nurseries they, transplant them.
why correct: A semicolon correctly joins the two clauses.
tip: Use a period, semicolon, or comma + conjunction.

stem: “Hoping to finish the model before the deadline and working late every night” is a complete sentence.
options / answer: True | False
why correct: It contains only participial phrases; there is no subject and main verb.
tip: Long word groups can still be fragments.

stem: Which paragraph revision contains NO fragments or run-ons?
options / answer: A) The souq is old. Its arches carved. Shops sell spices. | B) The souq is old, its arches are carved, its shops sell spices. | C) The souq is old its arches are carved. | D) The souq is old. Its arches are carved, and its shops sell spices.
why correct: Each sentence is complete and correctly joined.
tip: Check every sentence in a paragraph.

stem: Choose the past tense: “The bell ____ at noon.”
options / answer: A) rings | B) rung | C) rang | D) ringed
why correct: ring → rang → rung.
tip: Past participle needs has/have/had.

stem: Match each verb with its past participle.
options / answer: freeze = frozen | steal = stolen | forgive = forgiven | shake = shaken
why correct: These verbs form the past participle with -en.
tip: Test with “I have ___.”

stem: Choose: “By the time we arrived, the guests had already ____.”
options / answer: A) went | B) goed | C) go | D) gone
why correct: had + gone (past participle of go).
tip: go → went → gone.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The coral |  had |  sank |  to the bottom.
why correct: After “had,” use the past participle “sunk.”
tip: sink → sank → (had) sunk.

stem: Which sentence uses lie/lay correctly?
options / answer: A) Yesterday the tired dog lay in the shade. | B) Yesterday the tired dog lied in the shade. | C) Yesterday the tired dog layed in the shade. | D) Yesterday the tired dog laid in the shade.
why correct: lie (rest) → lay (past). lay (put) → laid (past).
tip: Lie = recline; lay = put something down.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: Which word is an abstract noun? “Mariam’s loyalty surprised her brother.”
options / answer: A) surprised | B) loyalty | C) Mariam’s | D) brother
why correct: Loyalty is a quality, not something you touch.
tip: Abstract nouns name ideas and feelings.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: In “Mrs. Qadri gave Yusuf a cup,” what is “Yusuf”?
options / answer: A) the subject | B) the direct object | C) the indirect object | D) the verb
why correct: Yusuf receives the cup: indirect object.
tip: Gave WHAT? (direct) To WHOM? (indirect).

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: Which noun is used as a predicate noun? “The ladder was a gift.”
options / answer: A) a | B) was | C) ladder | D) gift
why correct: “Gift” follows the linking verb and renames the subject.
tip: Predicate nouns rename the subject.

skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective
stem: Which TWO words are nouns used as appositives? “My sister, a talented artist, painted the mural with Huda, her best friend.”
options / answer: A) friend | B) sister | C) artist | D) mural
why correct: “A talented artist” renames sister; “her best friend” renames Huda.
tip: Appositives rename nearby nouns.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: Choose the plural of “ox”: “Two strong ____ pulled the heavy cart.”
options / answer: A) oxen | B) oxes | C) oxs | D) ox’s
why correct: ox → oxen, an irregular plural from Old English.
tip: Irregular plurals: ox/oxen, child/children.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: What is the plural of “analysis”?
options / answer: A) analyses | B) analysises | C) analysis | D) analysi
why correct: Greek -is plurals change to -es: analysis → analyses.
tip: crisis → crises; thesis → theses.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: Match each singular noun with its plural.
options / answer: cactus = cacti | phenomenon = phenomena | criterion = criteria | larva = larvae
why correct: These plurals come from Latin and Greek.
tip: Learn academic plurals.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: Both |  of my brother-in-laws |  work |  at the port.
why correct: In compound nouns, pluralize the main word: brothers-in-law.
tip: Pluralize the important word in a compound noun.

skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns
stem: Which sentence uses plurals and possessives correctly?
options / answer: A) The scientists’ datas show that the reefs’ health is declining. | B) The scientists’ data show that the reefs’ health is declining. | C) The scientist’s data shows that the reef’s health are declining. | D) The scientists data show that the reefs health is declining.
why correct: Plural possessives (scientists’, reefs’) and the plural “data … show.”
tip: Check plurals, possessives and agreement together.

stem: Which sentence is an exclamation?
options / answer: A) Can you see the dunes? | B) The view from the dunes is wide. | C) What an incredible view from the dunes! | D) Look at the dunes.
why correct: It expresses strong feeling and ends with “!”.
tip: Exclamations show strong emotion.

stem: Which sentence is a simple sentence with a compound predicate?
options / answer: A) Mariam waved, and Yusuf smiled. | B) Mariam and Yusuf smiled. | C) When Mariam waved, Yusuf smiled. | D) Mariam waved and smiled.
why correct: One subject, two verbs, one clause.
tip: Simple sentences can have compound parts.

stem: Which sentence begins with an introductory prepositional phrase?
options / answer: A) Under the bright lanterns, the market came alive. | B) Bright lanterns lit the market. | C) The market, bright and busy, came alive. | D) The market came alive under the lanterns.
why correct: “Under the bright lanterns” opens the sentence.
tip: Varying sentence openings improves style.

stem: Which revision best combines these sentences with varied structure? “The tide rose. The boats lifted. The fishermen cheered.”
options / answer: A) Rising tide, lifting boats, cheering fishermen. | B) As the tide rose and the boats lifted, the fishermen cheered. | C) The tide rose and the boats lifted and the fishermen cheered. | D) The tide rose, the boats lifted, the fishermen cheered.
why correct: A dependent clause with a compound subject-verb pair creates variety.
tip: Combine choppy sentences for flow.

stem: Choose the present perfect: “Mariam ____ in the choir for two years.”
options / answer: A) sings | B) has sung | C) will sing | D) sang
why correct: has/have + past participle = present perfect.
tip: Present perfect connects past to now.

stem: Which sentence is in the future progressive tense?
options / answer: A) We sailed at noon. | B) We are sailing. | C) At noon tomorrow, we will be sailing. | D) We have sailed.
why correct: will be + -ing = future progressive.
tip: Progressive = ongoing action.

stem: Which sentence has a correct sequence of tenses?
options / answer: A) After Yusuf misses the bus, he walked home. | B) After Yusuf will miss the bus, he walked home. | C) After Yusuf had missed the bus, he walks home. | D) After Yusuf had missed the bus, he walked home.
why correct: Past perfect (had missed) shows the earlier past action.
tip: Use past perfect for the earlier of two past events.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: Every morning, Mariam |  walked |  to the bakery and |  buys bread.
why correct: Keep tenses consistent: walked … bought.
tip: Avoid unnecessary tense shifts.

stem: Which sentence uses verb mood correctly (subjunctive)?
options / answer: A) If I were the principal, I would keep the five-day week. | B) If I was the principal, I would keep the five-day week. | C) If I be the principal, I would keep the five-day week. | D) If I am the principal, I would keep the five-day week.
why correct: Unreal conditions use the subjunctive “were.”
tip: If I were… = imagining something not true.

stem: Which sentence correctly uses commas around an appositive?
options / answer: A) Mrs. Qadri the baker opened, the door. | B) Mrs. Qadri, the baker, opened the door. | C) Mrs. Qadri the baker, opened the door. | D) Mrs. Qadri, the baker opened the door.
why correct: Nonessential appositives are set off by commas on both sides.
tip: Two commas around extra information.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: My grandfather |  who planted the orchard |  built |  a ladder.
why correct: A nonrestrictive clause about a specific person needs commas on both sides.
tip: Extra information about a specific noun is set off by commas.

stem: Which sentence punctuates the quotation correctly?
options / answer: A) Mariam said “I knew you’d walk the bakery way.” | B) Mariam said, I knew you’d walk the bakery way. | C) Mariam said, “I knew you’d walk the bakery way.” | D) Mariam said, “i knew you’d walk the bakery way.”
why correct: Comma after the tag; capitalized quotation inside quotation marks.
tip: Tag, comma, “Quotation.”

stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates a question in dialogue?
options / answer: A) “Does that radio still work,” Sara asked. | B) Does that radio still work? Sara asked. | C) “Does that radio still work”? Sara asked. | D) “Does that radio still work?” Sara asked.
why correct: The question mark belongs to the quotation and goes inside.
tip: End marks stay with the spoken words.

stem: Which sentence correctly uses a quotation within a quotation?
options / answer: A) “My grandfather always said, ‘Some things last if you look after them,’” Sara explained. | B) ‘My grandfather always said, “Some things last…”’ Sara explained. | C) “My grandfather always said, “Some things last…,”” Sara explained. | D) “My grandfather always said, Some things last…,” Sara explained.
why correct: Use single quotation marks for a quotation inside a quotation.
tip: Double outside, single inside.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: “I came for a short article,” |  Sara said. |  “I’m leaving with a book” | .
why correct: The period belongs inside the closing quotation mark.
tip: Periods and commas go inside quotation marks.

stem: Which sentence correctly integrates a short quotation from a text?
options / answer: A) Huda argues that visitors come for “what is special about a place”. | B) Huda argues that visitors come for “what is special about a place.” | C) Huda argues that visitors come for “What is special about a place.” | D) Huda argues that visitors come for, “what is special about a place.”
why correct: A quoted fragment blends into your sentence without a comma or capital.
tip: Integrate quotations smoothly.

stem: Which word has the most NEGATIVE connotation for a crowded market?
options / answer: A) busy | B) lively | C) chaotic | D) bustling
why correct: “Chaotic” suggests disorder.
tip: Connotation = feeling a word carries.

stem: In “Desert Night,” why does the poet say the sand gives back heat “in slow, warm breaths”?
options / answer: A) To show it is cold | B) To describe a storm | C) To make the desert seem dangerous | D) To make the desert feel alive and comforting
why correct: “Breaths” and “warm” carry gentle, living connotations.
tip: Word choice shapes feeling.

stem: In “The Last Bus Home,” the battery is at “four percent” before the screen goes black. What does this suggest the screen did?
options / answer: A) turned off because the battery ran out | B) grew brighter | C) broke into pieces | D) showed a picture
why correct: Low battery + black screen = it shut off.
tip: Use cause clues nearby.

stem: In the coral article, “transplant them onto damaged reefs” most likely means…
options / answer: A) photograph them | B) move and plant them in a new place | C) throw them away | D) feed them to fish
why correct: They grow corals in nurseries, then move them to reefs.
tip: Use the purpose of the action.

stem: Read: “Mr. Aziz was so taciturn that he answered every question in six words or fewer.” What does taciturn mean?
options / answer: A) forgetful | B) very angry | C) saying very little | D) very talkative
why correct: The clue “six words or fewer” defines the word.
tip: Example clues show meaning.

passage: Letter to the Editor: Save the Old Souq
stem: In the souq letter, what does “heritage” mean in “protect our heritage”?
options / answer: A) tourist signs | B) lighting | C) modern shopping | D) traditions and history passed down from earlier generations
why correct: Huda links the souq to her grandfather and city history.
tip: Use surrounding ideas to define abstract words.

stem: Read: “Despite the meager harvest, the farmers shared what little they had.” What does meager mean, and which clue helps most?
options / answer: A) very small; “what little they had” | B) very large; “the farmers shared” | C) late; “Despite” | D) delicious; “harvest”
why correct: “What little they had” restates the meaning.
tip: Restatement clues repeat the meaning in other words.

stem: “A camel groans, low as a cello string.” What kind of figurative language is this?
options / answer: A) metaphor | B) simile | C) hyperbole | D) idiom
why correct: A comparison using “as” is a simile.
tip: Simile = like/as.

passage: Starting Over: A Story and a Poem
stem: In “Transplant,” the tree “bowed its narrow head.” What does this personification suggest?
options / answer: A) The tree was angry. | B) The tree was praying. | C) The tree seemed sad and weak after being moved. | D) The tree was growing fast.
why correct: Giving the tree a human gesture shows it struggling.
tip: Personification = human traits for things.

stem: The Latin root “struct” means build. What does “reconstruct” mean?
options / answer: A) look again | B) break apart | C) write again | D) build again
why correct: re (again) + struct (build).
tip: Combine prefix and root.

stem: Match each root with its meaning.
options / answer: rupt = break | ject = throw | cred = believe | mal = bad
why correct: These roots appear in erupt, project, credible and malfunction.
tip: Think of a word with each root.

stem: Using roots, what does “incredible” literally mean, and how is it used in everyday speech?
options / answer: A) “not believable”; people use it to mean amazing | B) “able to be thrown”; it means far | C) “very believable”; it means boring | D) “badly built”; it means broken
why correct: in (not) + cred (believe) + ible (able to be).
tip: Roots give literal meaning; usage can extend it.

stem: Choose: “The camel walked across the ____.”
options / answer: A) dessert | B) dezert | C) desert | D) deserts’
why correct: A desert is a dry land; a dessert is a sweet.
tip: Dessert has two s’s like “sweet stuff.”

stem: In which sentence does “tear” rhyme with “bear”?
options / answer: A) A tear ran down her cheek. | B) Be careful not to tear the map. | C) She wiped away a tear. | D) The tear in her eye sparkled.
why correct: To tear (rip) rhymes with bear.
tip: Homographs may differ in sound.

stem: “The coral may die in a minute amount of warmer water over many weeks.” How is “minute” pronounced and what does it mean?
options / answer: A) MIN-it; sixty seconds | B) MIN-it; very small | C) my-NOOT; very small | D) my-NOOT; sixty seconds
why correct: Minute (my-NOOT) means tiny.
tip: Use context to choose meaning and sound.

stem: Which sentence uses “refuse” to mean garbage?
options / answer: A) They refuse the offer. | B) Do not refuse help. | C) I refuse to give up. | D) The workers collected the refuse from the market.
why correct: REF-use (noun) = garbage; re-FUSE (verb) = decline.
tip: Part of speech changes meaning and stress.

stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.
options / answer: The council’s |  plan will |  effect |  the whole city.
why correct: “Affect” is the verb meaning to influence; “effect” is usually a noun (result).
tip: Affect = action (verb); effect = end result (noun).

stem: What does “bite off more than you can chew” mean?
options / answer: A) take on more than you can handle | B) eat too fast | C) share food | D) be very hungry
why correct: It warns against taking on too much.
tip: Idioms have nonliteral meanings.

stem: After the coach gave his offer, he said, “The ball is in your court.” What did he mean?
options / answer: A) Go play tennis. | B) It is your turn to decide. | C) You lost the game. | D) The court is closed.
why correct: The decision is now the other person’s.
tip: Use the situation to interpret.

stem: Missing the bus turned out to be “a blessing in disguise” for Yusuf. Why?
options / answer: A) He avoided homework. | B) He got home faster. | C) It led him to discover how much his sister cared. | D) He found money on the road.
why correct: Something bad (missing the bus) led to something good.
tip: Connect the idiom to story events.

passage: Letter to the Editor: Save the Old Souq
stem: Which adage BEST fits Huda’s letter about saving the souq?
options / answer: A) “Haste makes waste.” | B) “The early bird catches the worm.” | C) “Too many cooks spoil the broth.” | D) “You don’t know what you’ve got until it’s gone.”
why correct: Huda warns that the souq’s value will be lost if it is torn down.
tip: Match the adage to the main message.

stem: Match each saying with its meaning.
options / answer: Every cloud has a silver lining = something good can come from bad | The pen is mightier than the sword = words can be more powerful than force | Costs an arm and a leg = very expensive | When in Rome, do as the Romans do = follow local customs
why correct: Each saying carries a lesson or comment about life.
tip: Think of situations where each fits.

stem: Which resource tells you the origin (etymology) of a word?
options / answer: A) a dictionary entry’s etymology section | B) a calendar | C) an index | D) an atlas
why correct: Many dictionaries show where a word came from.
tip: Etymology = word history.

stem: A dictionary lists “con·tent (n.) KON-tent: what is inside; (adj.) kuhn-TENT: satisfied.” Which fits “Mariam was content to wait”?
options / answer: A) Neither | B) kuhn-TENT, satisfied | C) KON-tent, what is inside | D) Both
why correct: Here it describes Mariam, so it is the adjective.
tip: Use part of speech to choose the entry.

stem: When would a thesaurus be MORE useful than a dictionary?
options / answer: A) when you need a word’s origin | B) when you need a pronunciation | C) when you want a more precise word with a similar meaning | D) when you need a definition
why correct: Thesauruses list synonyms and antonyms.
tip: Choose the tool for the task.

stem: Put these words in dictionary order.
options / answer: coral → corridor → cottage → council → counsel
why correct: Compare letters in order: cor-a, cor-r, cot, coun-c, coun-s.
tip: Keep comparing until letters differ.

stem: Which word is the strongest synonym for “tired”?
options / answer: A) restful | B) energetic | C) sleepy | D) exhausted
why correct: Exhausted means extremely tired.
tip: Synonyms vary in intensity.
